## Research goal, normalization, and stable scope [Steps 1–3, 28–36]

The human’s highest goal has remained unchanged: decide the full Yau Problem 26 statement for every \(n\ge2\), namely whether dimension-only constants \(c_n<C_n\) can be chosen so that every closed connected smooth \(n\)-manifold carrying a metric with
\[
c_ng\le \operatorname{Ric}_g\le C_ng
\]
also carries some Einstein metric, ultimately with a complete independently checkable proof or disproof and Lean 4 formalization [Step 1].

The first normalization split the problem into neighborhoods of \(+I\) and \(-I\). Because the interval constants are existential and may have either sign, a topology-independent Einstein-forcing neighborhood around either sign would suffice in a fixed dimension. Conversely, a disproof must defeat every possible interval; constructing a bad family near only one sign does not by itself refute the proposition [Steps 1–3].

Most of the session developed a restricted four-dimensional negative-Ricci laboratory based on LeBrun/Ishida–LeBrun manifolds. Its purpose is to test whether known all-sign Einstein-obstructed topologies can nevertheless support metrics with \(\operatorname{Ric}\to-g\), and, increasingly, to prove a quantitative negative defect gap for that family. Even successful completion would not settle arbitrary four-manifolds, the positive branch, dimensions \(n\ge5\), the original all-dimensional interval proposition, or Lean formalization [Steps 1–36].

## Primary-source survey and early route filtering [Steps 1–3]

The initial literature pass used `Skills/qiushi-yau26/references/research/20260910.tex` and primary or near-primary sources on Min-Oo, Lohkamp, LeBrun, prescribed Ricci curvature, Ricci-flow stability, and four-dimensional topology. Min-Oo’s bounded-geometry hypothesis was corrected after an OCR error: the relevant scale-invariant term is \(d^2\max|K|\), not the previously transcribed expression involving \(r^{-2}\max|K|\). Thus an almost-negative-Einstein sequence can evade Min-Oo through diameter growth as well as curvature-scale degeneration [Steps 1–2].

Lohkamp’s `RICCI CURVATURE MODULO HOMOTOPY` and `Curvature Contents` support one-sided Ricci inequalities, local Ricci-decreasing deformation, and \(h\)-principle phenomena, but the recovered sources do not construct two-sided operator pinching \(\operatorname{Ric}\approx-g\) on arbitrary closed manifolds. DeTurck and prescribed-Ricci results were likewise local or restricted-global. The initially attractive direct flexibility counterexample was therefore replaced by the harder question of whether local two-jet flexibility can be made compatible with the global topology and curvature budgets imposed by two-sided pinching [Steps 1–2].

Kröncke-type theorems were classified as dynamical stability near a pre-existing Einstein metric rather than topology-independent existence results. Primary recovery remained incomplete for the exact original printed text of Yau’s Problem 26, Anderson 1989 Corollary B(4), and Ye 1993; no inaccessible hypothesis was treated as verified [Steps 1–2].

Dimension three was retained as a benchmark. Since \(W=0\), tight Ricci pinching controls sectional curvature, connecting the positive side to Hamilton and spherical space forms and the negative side to hyperbolic/geometrization mechanisms. This dimension-specific behavior did not provide a higher-dimensional route [Steps 2–3].

## Four-dimensional topology candidates and abandoned construction shortcuts [Steps 1–5]

The main candidate family became
\[
M=X\#k\overline{\mathbb{CP}}^{\,2},
\qquad A=c_1^2(X),
\]
and its Ishida–LeBrun multi-summand variants, where \(X\) is built from minimal complex surfaces of general type. These were preferred to elementary Hitchin–Thorpe violators because suitable members remain strictly Hitchin–Thorpe compatible while Seiberg–Witten theory still obstructs Einstein metrics. Equality or violating families already have elementary Chern–Weil gaps against arbitrarily tight Ricci pinching and are poor candidates for a vanishing-defect sequence [Steps 1–2].

Connected-sum arithmetic was repaired:
\[
\chi(\#_m\mathbb{CP}^2)=m+2,\qquad
\tau=m,\qquad
2\chi-3\tau=4-m.
\]
Thus \(m=4\) is the equality case, \(m\ge5\) violates Hitchin–Thorpe, and \(m=3\) does not. Later positive-branch candidate discussions were required to use this correction [Steps 3–4].

Positive-Ricci constructions of Reiser, Burdick, and related core-metric work showed that many connected sums carry \(\operatorname{Ric}>0\), but no family was verified to combine all-sign Einstein obstruction, strict Hitchin–Thorpe compatibility, and arbitrarily small positive Einstein defect. Positive Ricci existence alone never became evidence against the positive branch [Steps 1–3, 8–9].

An orbifold/ALE desingularization route was developed with S0910A03. A bare-core scaling argument initially suggested that a nonzero gluing obstruction stays order one in normalized Ricci defect. This was corrected: an \(O(t^2)\) relative correction to a \(t^2\)-scaled Ricci-flat core can produce order-one Ricci curvature. The surviving issue is therefore linearized solvability and Cauchy-data matching, requiring vanishing of the first and higher gluing obstructions plus an independent all-sign topology obstruction [Steps 1, 3–4].

A straightforward Kähler blow-up route was excluded. If a blow-up metric were Kähler and negatively pinched with defect below one, its Ricci form would be negative on an exceptional curve, contradicting \(c_1(TM)\cdot E_j=1\). Any construction approaching \(\operatorname{Ric}=-g\) on these blow-ups must be genuinely non-Kähler [Steps 3–4].

## Mixed Seiberg–Witten reduction to the near-critical regime [Steps 2–8, 29–30]

The first quantitative estimate combined LeBrun’s scalar-curvature inequality with Chern–Gauss–Bonnet and
\[
\delta_\sigma=\|g^{-1}\operatorname{Ric}-\sigma I\|_{\infty,\mathrm{op}}.
\]
It yielded a positive negative-branch gap for each fixed topology, but the scalar-only gap could decay like \(A^{-1/2}\). This established the essential distinction between a fixed-topology gap and exclusion of a varying-topology counterexample sequence. The calculations were checked in `scripts/verify_bounds.py` and recorded in the Step 2 analysis notes [Step 2].

The decisive refinement used the mixed Seiberg–Witten inequality
\[
\frac1{4\pi^2}\int_M\left(\frac{s^2}{24}+2|W^+|^2\right)d\mu
\ge \frac23(a^+)^2.
\]
For a sign-selected monopole class with \((a^+)^2\ge A\), Chern–Gauss–Bonnet and trace-free Ricci control give
\[
\frac{\delta_-}{1-\delta_-}
\ge
\sqrt{\frac{k/A-1/3}{2}}.
\]
The coefficients and Chern–Gauss–Bonnet normalization were independently repaired and checked in `notes/step3_mixed_bound_analysis.md`, `notes/step3_complete_analysis.md`, and `scripts/mixed_sw_bound_analysis.py` [Step 3].

This changed the topology search. Every family with \(k/A\) bounded strictly above \(1/3\), including earlier proposals with \(k/A\ge2/3\), has a topology-uniform negative defect gap from topology alone. Only sequences satisfying
\[
k/A\to1/3
\]
can remain difficult. The value \(1/3\) is the boundary of the available obstruction, not a proved transition to existence [Steps 3–4].

The sign-selection argument explains why \((a^+)^2\ge A\) is possible although \(a^2=A-k\): averaging over the monopole family adds self-dual projections of exceptional classes. Near-criticality would force many exceptional directions to become nearly anti-self-dual. This was not converted into an intersection-form contradiction because abstract positive subspaces can be orthogonal to exceptional directions; any further consequence must use the geometry of the pinched metrics and the actual Seiberg–Witten inequalities [Steps 3–4].

The bookkeeping was reorganized as
\[
I=\frac1{4\pi^2}\int\left(\frac{s^2}{24}+2|W^+|^2\right),\quad
J=\frac1{4\pi^2}\int\frac{|\mathring{\operatorname{Ric}}|^2}{2},
\]
\[
q=k-\frac A3,\qquad
D_a=I-\frac23(a^+)^2,
\]
with
\[
D_a
=
J-q-\frac23\big((a^+)^2-A\big),
\qquad
0\le D_a\le J-q.
\]
Together with a volume estimate independent of extra Noether assumptions, a hypothetical sequence with \(A_i\to\infty\), \(\delta_i\to0\), and \(k_i/A_i\to1/3\) satisfies
\[
q/A=O(\delta^2),\qquad
\operatorname{Vol}/A=O(1),\qquad
J/A=O(\delta^2),\qquad
D_a/A\to0.
\]
These are topology-normalized statements; claims that \(D_a\to0\) absolutely or that every pointed limit saturates the inequality were withdrawn [Steps 4–8].

A later attempt to split the family into “topological above-critical” and “exact critical” cases was narrowed. The topological estimate gives a gap proportional to \(\sqrt{q/A}\), but this loses its margin along sequences with \(q_i>0\) and \(q_i/A_i\to0\). Thus the analytic smoothing route must cover the entire near-critical regime, not only the exact locus \(q=0\) [Steps 29–30].

## Near-equality geometry and the forbidden calibrated Einstein germ [Steps 5–8]

The final Cauchy–Schwarz stage in LeBrun’s argument was expanded into
\[
\int_M\big(s+8\sqrt6\,|W^+|\big)^2\,d\mu
\le864\pi^2D_a.
\]
Negative pinching forces \(s\to-4\), so the topology-normalized bulk approaches
\[
|W^+|=\frac1{2\sqrt6},
\qquad
|W^+|^2=\frac1{24}.
\]
This excluded a model with a macroscopic negative Kähler–Einstein exterior and negligible-volume topological insertions: for \(\operatorname{Ric}=-g\), a Kähler–Einstein four-metric has \(|W^+|^2=2/3\) and contributes a fixed positive remainder density [Step 5].

Norm control alone was initially overinterpreted as control of the full \(W^+\) spectrum. If \(\alpha\ge\beta\ge w\) are its eigenvalues, then
\[
|W^+|^2-\frac32w^2=\frac12(\alpha-\beta)^2.
\]
The calibrated spectrum
\[
(-1/6,1/12,1/12)
\]
therefore requires control of the lowest-eigenvalue substitution slack as well as the norm remainder. It is one quarter of the corresponding \(\operatorname{Ric}=-g\) Kähler–Einstein spectrum \((-2/3,1/3,1/3)\) [Steps 6–8].

The missing tensor slack was encoded by the nonnegative density
\[
f=\frac23s-2\sqrt{\frac23}|W^+|,
\qquad
b=\frac23s+2w,
\qquad
G=f^2-(b_-)^2,
\]
for which
\[
\int G\le48\pi^2D_a.
\]
At \(s=-4\), \(|W^+|^2=1/24\), and \(G=0\), the spectrum is exactly \((-1/6,1/12,1/12)\). The algebra was checked in the Step 6 and Step 8 scripts [Step 8].

Derdziński’s original 1983 paper was recovered at `data/sources/derdzinski_1983_self_dual_kahler_einstein_four.pdf`, with extracted text in the corresponding source note. Proposition 5 states that on \(\{W^+\ne0\}\), if \(\delta W^+=0\) and \(W^+\) has at most two eigenvalues, then
\[
(24|W^+|^2)^{1/3}g
\]
is locally Kähler. At calibrated constant norm the conformal factor is constant. Hence an Einstein germ with the calibrated spectrum would itself be locally Kähler, but a negative Kähler–Einstein four-metric has the incompatible norm \(2/3\). This became the local forbidden-germ contradiction [Steps 6–8].

An intervening detour treated Derdziński’s conformal factor as an arbitrary scalar solution and wrongly concluded that noncompact limits defeated the argument. This was corrected because the factor is geometrically determined by the Weyl eigenvalue. The final contradiction is through the locally conformally Kähler/modulus incompatibility, not through an unsupported assertion that \(\nabla W^+=0\) or that the eigenframe is globally fixed [Steps 7–8, 29–31].

## Compactness, cover transport, and the evolution of the collapse question [Steps 7–14]

The first compactness plan attempted to pass to smooth global limits and invoke compact almost-Kähler rigidity. It failed because topology, volume, and diameter can diverge, normalized deficits can escape spatially, and noncompact pointed limits do not satisfy compact rigidity hypotheses [Steps 5–6].

The harmonic-coordinate passage was reformulated correctly: on a region with uniform harmonic radius, bounded Ricci and suitable finite-\(p\) curvature control give strong enough convergence through the harmonic-coordinate Ricci equation; the weak Einstein limit can then be bootstrapped to smoothness. Automatic \(C^{2,\alpha}\) convergence of the approximating metrics was withdrawn [Steps 7–8].

A volume-random basepoint argument gave a measure-scale collapse conclusion. For every fixed \(v>0\), the volume fraction of points with \(\operatorname{Vol}(B_1(p))\ge v\) tends to zero in a hypothetical near-critical sequence; otherwise a volume-typical noncollapsed ball with vanishing local deficits would converge to the forbidden germ. This does not imply \(\sup_p\operatorname{Vol}(B_1(p))\to0\), since bounded-volume noncollapsed islands can survive with negligible global measure [Step 8].

A general cover-mean lemma replaced model-specific lattice counting. For a buffered normal cover
\[
\pi:(\widehat U,\hat g)\to(U,g),
\]
with \(\operatorname{Ric}\ge-(n-1)Kg\) and \(B_{3r}(\hat p)\) inside the cover,
\[
\fint_{B_r(\hat p)}\pi^*\phi
\le
\frac{V_K(3r)}{V_K(r)}
\fint_{B_r(p)}\phi
\]
for nonnegative \(\phi\). Its proof used a Borel section, deck-transform counting, disjoint translated sections, and Bishop–Gromov comparison. It requires a genuine normal deck action, a precompact buffer, and a measurable section; it does not automatically apply to truncated pseudogroups [Step 9].

The obstruction was reframed around “buffered chart accessibility”: any mechanism yielding a fixed-radius controlled chart can be combined with mean-defect transport and the forbidden germ. Naber–Zhang is only one sufficient source. Direct source checking showed that its harmonic-radius conclusion requires low residual dimension, lower model noncollapse scale, maximal fibered nilpotency rank, and local completeness. Stronger curvature conclusions need Einstein or \(\nabla\operatorname{Ric}\) control. Cheeger–Naber’s cited theorem was corrected to a four-dimensional finiteness theorem with diameter and noncollapse assumptions, not an all-dimensional Einstein-existence theorem [Steps 10–11].

Several collapse-model “obstructions” were corrected. The Bianchi II/Nil\(^3\) orbit-volume equation is
\[
v''=(3-\mu)v,
\qquad
\mu=\frac{a_3^2}{2a_1^2a_2^2},
\]
not \(v''=(3+\mu)v\); the complex-hyperbolic cusp supplied the counter-calibration. Lott’s orbit-volume equation can obstruct only with global hypotheses such as parabolicity, bounded orbit volume, periodicity, endpoint control, and determinant-line holonomy. It does not prohibit local nilpotent Einstein symmetry [Steps 9–10].

A coordinate Christoffel/Riemann calculation in `scripts/step12_taub_nut_ads_coordinate_curvature.py`, independently checked by S0910A03, verified the Taub–NUT–AdS Einstein metric and its U(2)-symmetric Weyl spectrum. Core-containing fixed-radius balls can have collapsed local universal covers because the short Hopf circle contracts through the NUT, whereas smaller annular Hopf-trivializing domains avoid the core and approach real hyperbolic four-space. Thus collapse of a prescribed core-containing domain does not rule out all smaller accessible charts [Steps 11–12].

The multiscale computation further showed that core-containing regions have diverging mean full-Weyl energy, while accessible annuli are macroscopically uncalibrated. A reversed-orientation shell can hit the calibrated norm at a single radius but has the wrong eigenvalue pattern and nonzero integrated defect. A single radius cannot contradict Derdziński, whose conclusion concerns an open Einstein region [Step 12].

The four-dimensional topological identities were repaired before averaging:

## Fixed-scale smoothing and the failure of naive localization [Steps 14–18]

Ye Li’s four-dimensional smoothing theorem was revisited. The original objection that a nonzero Einstein background prevents small-energy smoothing was incorrect: Li’s condition is dimensionless,
\[
r^4\fint_{B_r(x)}|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\le\varepsilon_{\rm Li}.
\]
On maximal-function good sets, the global Chern–Weil/Noether budget gives a local mean bound, so choosing a sufficiently small fixed physical radius makes the dimensionless quantity small while preserving the \(\operatorname{Ric}\approx-g\) scale [Step 14].

Li’s theorem is complete and all-centers, not a selected-ball local theorem. The promising four-dimensional cancellation was
\[
A_R\lesssim\frac{R^2}{\operatorname{Vol}(B_R)^{1/2}},
\qquad
\|\operatorname{Rm}\|_{L^2(B_R)}
\lesssim\sqrt{K_0\operatorname{Vol}(B_R)},
\]
so the critical product is independent of collapsed volume. This motivated a cutoff flow
\[
\partial_tg=-2\chi^2(\operatorname{Ric}+g)
\]
on selected supports [Steps 14–15].

Step 15 combined maximal-function good sets, Vitali selection, separated supports, plateaux, the homogeneity of \(E=\operatorname{Ric}+g\), and terminal topological recalibration. It nevertheless declared localization complete for invalid reasons. Ricci flow has no finite propagation, and Li’s bootstrap supremum ranges over all centers in the working region; controlling only an inner center set does not close the inner/outer inequality. Agreement across sessions based on the same argument was not independent verification [Steps 15–16].

The completion claim was withdrawn in `notes/step15_cutoff_smoothing_architecture.md` and the route assessment. The target became transition-inclusive: control metric comparability, Sobolev geometry, curvature energy, unweighted defect, and continuation on the whole active support, while retaining every cutoff derivative term. Homogeneity prevents a curvature-only source in the defect equation, but does not automatically prevent amplification of a small nonzero defect [Step 16].

A harmonic-form/eigenline shortcut was also rejected. A global harmonic form may have negligible mass on every chosen chart, and the harmonic representative of a monopole class is not simply the self-dual form used in the Seiberg–Witten proof. Unique continuation gives no uniform local mass lower bound. Terminal completion-square and tensor-gap densities remained the direct calibration mechanism [Step 16].

## Exponential pullback as the downstream collapse bypass [Steps 16–18, 27–28]

Once bounded-sectional-curvature buffers are available, exponential pullback can replace much of the local fundamental-group classification. Rauch Jacobian comparison and Liouville invariance of geodesic flow transfer small mean nonnegative deficit densities from the base to tangent-space exponential balls. The pulled-back domain is noncollapsed by Rauch even when the exponential map is highly noninjective in the base [Steps 16–17].

This was initially left alongside a proposed Euler/F-structure plateau-noncollapse problem. Step 28 corrected the route: Euler-density localization and base injectivity-radius bounds are unnecessary if the smoothing theorem supplies inner plateau centers \(P_i\) with
\[
\operatorname{Vol}(P_i)\ge\alpha A_i
\]
and fixed-radius bounded-curvature buffers. For a nonnegative terminal density \(D_i\),
\[
\int_{P_i}\fint_{\text{exp-pullback ball}}D_i
\le C(K,\rho)\int_{M_i}D_i.
\]
Thus \(\int D_i=o(A_i)\) selects a center with vanishing pulled-back mean. A radius shrink and harmonic-coordinate compactness then give the forbidden Einstein germ [Step 28].

Terminal calibration was made explicit rather than transported by \(C^0\) comparison. On the terminal metric let
\[
E=\operatorname{Ric}+g,\qquad Q=\int|E|^2.
\]
The orthogonal splitting gives
\[
\int(s+4)^2\le4Q,\qquad
J\le \frac{Q}{8\pi^2}.
\]
For the selected monopole sign and \(q\ge0\), the exact identity gives \(0\le D_a\le J\). Reapplying the completion-square and tensor-gap estimates yields
\[
\int(s+8\sqrt6|W^+|)^2\le108Q,\qquad
\int G\le6Q.
\]
Hence the combined Einstein, scalar, modulus, and spectral deficit has integral at most \(119Q\) in the chosen normalization. These constants were checked in `scripts/step28_terminal_pullback_constants.py` [Step 28].

The downstream geometry is therefore no longer the main unresolved issue. It is conditional on sequence-uniform bounded-curvature plateau buffers, normalized plateau volume, and \(Q(T)/A\to0\), all of which must be produced upstream by the selected-support flow [Steps 28, 30, 36].

## Degenerate cutoff flow, weighted quantities, and normalization corrections [Steps 18–25]

The cutoff problem was recast with
\[
a=\chi^2,\qquad E=\operatorname{Ric}+g,\qquad
\partial_tg=-2aE.
\]
Weighted curvature \(a\operatorname{Rm}\), weighted velocity \(aE\), and the unweighted defect \(Q=\int|E|^2\) have different roles. A bound on \(aE\) does not control \(Q\) near \(a=0\), so terminal recalibration requires a separate unweighted estimate [Step 18].

Scalar algebra showed why \(a=\chi^2\) is structurally useful:
\[
\frac{|\nabla a|^2}{a}=4|\nabla\chi|^2.
\]
For weighted curvature \(f=aK\), quadratic reaction becomes \(cf^2\), not \(cf^2/a\). The full tensor equation nevertheless contains Hessian-\(a\), gradient-\(a\), moving-norm, and moving-volume terms, so this cancellation alone did not prove smoothing [Step 18].

A Whitney-scale representation used balls of radius \(\ell=cr\chi_0\). On such balls \(a/a_0\) has bounded ellipticity ratio, physical time \(r^2\) corresponds to fixed rescaled diffusion time, and the critical Sobolev reaction product is independent of \(\chi_0\) and collapsed volume [Step 19]. This exposed the right scale but also led to several corrections.

Direct all-exponent critical absorption was rejected because coefficients grow with the power \(p\). The route changed to fixed \(q=2\), parabolic Sobolev, fixed \(q=3\), and then positive-time Moser iteration. Any defect inequality with an additive curvature-only dissipation remainder was also rejected because integrating an \(O(A)\) curvature budget would leave an \(O(A)\), not \(o(A)\), error. The defect system must remain triangular, with curvature multiplying \(E^2\) and no source independent of \(E\) [Step 20].

A scaling mistake in a terminal Stampacchia estimate was corrected: under \(\tilde g=\ell^{-2}g\),
\[
|\operatorname{Rm}(\tilde g)|=\ell^2|\operatorname{Rm}(g)|.
\]
A subsequent, more basic normalization error was also found. A volume-normalized energy bound on an outer support does not imply the same bound on a smaller Whitney ball; the smaller mean can grow like \((r/\ell)^4\). Valid quantities are the dimensionless local energy and Sobolev-energy product, not a uniform Whitney-volume-normal \(L^2\) mean [Steps 21–22].

A graph system using weighted moments and neighbor matrices was explored. It could conditionally propagate componentwise energies under an all-centers critical smallness hypothesis, but a maximal net over all \(M\) includes bad centers. The graph theorem was therefore retained only as a conditional result and not used for the actual LeBrun sequence [Steps 22–24].

The route returned to individually selected buffered supports. The physical cutoff \(\chi\) has its entire transition region in a domain where an auxiliary energy cutoff \(\eta=1\), while \(\operatorname{supp}\nabla\eta\) lies in an open collar where \(\chi=0\). Thus
\[
a|\nabla\eta|^2=0,\qquad
\nabla a\cdot\nabla\eta=0,
\]
and the outer collar is exactly stationary. This is a support identity, not finite propagation [Step 24].

At a selected good center, the full auxiliary support has controlled initial \(L^2\) curvature and relative Sobolev coefficient. The active critical parameter is volume-independent after cancellation:
\[
\gamma\sim C_S K_2(0)^{1/2}\lesssim r^2\sqrt{K_0},
\]
in the squared Sobolev convention used later. The physical radius must be chosen after support ratios and tensor constants [Steps 24, 30–34].

The q=2 curvature calculation classified the principal Bochner term, first-derivative cutoff terms, Hessian-\(a\) terms, algebraic curvature coupling, moving inverse metric, and moving volume. An early statement that the normalized \(-2ag\) term provides curvature damping was withdrawn. For the pure conformal flow \(g(t)=e^{-2t}g_0\), \(|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\) grows as \(e^{4t}\) and \(d\mu\) shrinks as \(e^{-4t}\), so the four-dimensional curvature integral is invariant [Step 25].

## Weighted Moser development and successive repairs [Steps 26–34]

To control full-support metric drift, Step 26 introduced
\[
V(t)=\int_0^t\|aE(s)\|_{L^\infty(\operatorname{supp}\chi)}\,ds,
\]
which gives
\[
e^{-2V(t)}g_0\le g(t)\le e^{2V(t)}g_0.
\]
Plateau curvature alone cannot preserve transition-region Sobolev and energy geometry; support-wide weighted velocity is necessary [Step 26].

The fixed-power defect energy
\[
J_p=\int\eta^2a^{p-2}|E|^p
\]
and its dissipation were introduced. For \(p=6\),
\[
J_6=\int\eta^2\chi^8|E|^6.
\]
Yang’s local-flow source was read directly. Its DeTurck construction transports the cutoff coefficient and pulls back to the fixed spatial coefficient. Appendix B showed the same weight pattern as the desired defect iteration, but direct black-box invocation was withheld because the tensor Hessian-\(a\) contractions do not automatically reduce to Yang’s scalar assumptions [Step 26].

Step 27 proposed a unified weak Moser hierarchy using
\[
H_p=\int a^{p-2}f^p,\qquad
z_p=a^{(p-1)/2}f^{p/2},
\]
and the three-factor identity
\[
a^{p-1}Ff^p
=
(aF^3)^{1/3}(a^{p-2}f^p)^{1/3}z_p^{4/3}.
\]
This correctly identified polynomial \(p\)-loss as compatible with a geometric-exponent Moser product, but its first recurrence and exponent bookkeeping were incomplete [Step 27].

Step 28 corrected the reciprocal-exponent calculation and replaced a per-exponent Gronwall scheme by a nested time-cutoff recurrence. Fixed \(J_6\) persistence was explicitly separated from positive-time q=3 estimates. This was an important consolidation, but the recurrence still contained a hidden embedding issue [Step 28].

Step 29 interpreted a half-power mismatch between \(\|z_p\|_3^3\) and the next weighted moment as fatal and proposed ordinary unweighted Moser on
\[
U=a(\operatorname{Rm}+G).
\]
Both conclusions were corrected. Renaming the unknown does not remove the degeneracy of the operator \(a\Delta\), and the quadratic shifted-curvature reaction is \(U*U\), not \(aU*U\). \(U\) remains valuable for continuation, but cannot manufacture the first weighted curvature bound through uniformly parabolic Moser [Steps 29–30].

The actual repair is the mixed interpolation
\[
H_{3p/2}
=
\int (a^{p-2}f^p)^{1/2}z_p^2
\le H_p^{1/2}\|z_p\|_4^2.
\]
In the squared-norm Sobolev convention
\[
\|z\|_4^2
\le C_S\left(\|\nabla z\|_2^2+r^{-2}\|z\|_2^2\right),
\qquad
C_S\lesssim\frac{r^2}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Vol}}},
\]
the nested spacetime recurrence has
\[
A_{k+1}
\le C p_k^N C_S L_k^{3/2}A_k^{3/2},
\qquad
p_{k+1}=\frac32p_k,
\qquad
L_k\lesssim Cp_k^N4^k(t^{-1}+r^{-2}).
\]
The earlier \(L_k^{-1/2}\) factor was spurious [Steps 30–32].

A proposed volume-independent unnormalized Dirichlet Sobolev constant was rejected. On \(B^3(r)\times S^1(\varepsilon)\), a compactly supported function constant along the short circle forces the squared Sobolev coefficient to grow like \(\varepsilon^{-1/2}\). Vanishing at the support boundary ensures admissibility, not a collapse-independent coefficient. The intended mechanism is cancellation between \(C_S\) and the support-volume seed [Step 32].

Conditional on the fixed-exponent estimates, the repaired recurrence yields
\[
\|af(t)\|_\infty
\le
C C_S^{2/p_0}t^{-3/p_0}
\left(\int_{t/2}^tH_{p_0}(f)\right)^{1/p_0},
\]
up to the controlled \(r^{-2}\) and polynomial factors. Thus the expected endpoint forms were restored:
\[
\|aF(t)\|_\infty\lesssim\frac{\gamma}{t},
\qquad
\|aE(t)\|_\infty
\lesssim
\delta\left(\frac{r^2}{t}\right)^{1/3}.
\]
The latter is integrable at zero and gives drift \(O(\delta r^2\theta^{2/3})\). These remain conditional outputs, not a completed smoothing theorem [Steps 32–34].

## Fixed-exponent q=2/q=3 mechanism and the improved defect seed [Steps 33–34]

Step 33 attempted an explicit general-\(p\) curvature and defect hierarchy and found a useful integrated-potential mechanism. Its first tensor derivation still contained inconsistencies: it tried to integrate by parts an absolute value \(|\nabla^2a|\), used the wrong pre-absorption radial dissipation coefficient, controlled moving volume by unpropagated pointwise pinching, and failed the pure-scaling test. These faults were recorded rather than hidden by successful exponent scripts [Steps 33–34].

The q=3 mechanism was then separated cleanly from the full tensor derivation. The correct localized q=2 energy is
\[
K_2^\eta=\int\eta^2F^2,
\]
not the formal \(p=2\) member of \(a^{p-2}F^p\). With
\[
Y=\int\eta^2aF^3,
\qquad
\gamma=C_S(0)\big(K_2^\eta(0)\big)^{1/2},
\]
q=2 interpolation gives
\[
Y\le C\gamma(D_2^\eta+r^{-2}K_2^\eta).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\int_0^tY(s)\,ds\le C\gamma K_2^\eta(0),
\qquad
B(t):=\int_0^tC_S(s)^2Y(s)\,ds\le C\gamma^3
\]
inside the provisional first-exit regime [Step 34].

If the fixed \(p=3\) calculation gives
\[
Y'\le C(1+r^{-2}+C_S^2Y)Y,
\]
a good slice \(\tau\in[t/4,t/2]\) satisfies \(Y(\tau)\le C\gamma K_2^\eta(0)/t\). Ordinary Gronwall from \(\tau\) to \(t\), using the independently bounded integral \(B(t)\), gives
\[
Y(t)\le C\frac{\gamma K_2^\eta(0)}{t}.
\]
The appearance of \(Y\) in its own coefficient is therefore not circular. This fixed-exponent Gronwall is distinct from the later high-\(p\) nested-time Moser recurrence [Step 34].

The defect seed was simplified further through A03’s unregularized \(J_6\) calculation. Let
\[
s=|E|^2,\qquad
J_6=\int\eta^2a^4s^3,
\qquad
X_6=\int\eta^2a^5s^2|\nabla E|^2,
\qquad
w_6=\eta\chi^5|E|^3.
\]
No norm regularization is needed because \(s^3\) and \(w_6\) are smooth enough at \(E=0\). The potential is
\[
P_6=\int Fw_6^2.
\]
Two-factor Hölder and Sobolev give
\[
P_6\le C\gamma(X_6+r^{-2}J_6)
\]
using only the q=2 curvature seed. For small \(\gamma\),
\[
J_6'+cX_6\le C(1+r^{-2})J_6,
\]
so at \(T=\theta r^2\),
\[
J_6(T)\le C\delta^6\operatorname{Vol}.
\]
This superseded the Step 33 regularized three-factor \(J_6\) route and avoids integrating the nonintegrable curvature endpoint \(1/t\) from time zero [Step 34].

## Index-level curvature and defect contraction breakthrough [Step 35]

Step 35 returned to the geometric PDE and derived the Hessian-\(a\) contractions at the index level in the all-lower Riemann convention. This was the main advance that separated first smoothing estimates from pointwise control of the evolving cutoff Hessian [Step 35].

For \(h=-2aE\), the Hessian-\(a\) part of the all-lower Riemann variation reduces, after using pair symmetry and first-pair antisymmetry, to
\[
\Sigma_H^{\mathrm{Rm}}
=
8\,(\nabla_p\nabla_q a)\,B_{\mathrm{curv}}^{pq},
\qquad
B_{\mathrm{curv}}^{pq}
=
R^p{}_j{}^q{}_l E^{jl}.
\]
The product rule and contracted curvature identities give
\[
|\nabla B_{\mathrm{curv}}|
\le C F|\nabla\operatorname{Rm}|.
\]
This is exactly the derivative structure needed for signed tensor integration by parts. The Hessian contribution can be absorbed into
\[
\varepsilon p\big(D_p^{\mathrm{Rm}}+(p-2)D_p^F\big)
+
Cp^3r^{-2}K_p,
\]
without assuming a pointwise bound on \(\nabla^2a\) [Step 35].

The defect Hessian tensor was derived independently from the Ricci linearization. Writing \(\tau=\operatorname{tr}E\) and \(s=|E|^2\),
\[
(\partial_tE)_{\mathrm{Hess}\text{-}a}
=
(\Delta a)E
-(\nabla_i\nabla^la)E_{jl}
-(\nabla_j\nabla^la)E_{il}
+(\nabla_i\nabla_ja)\tau.
\]
Its contribution to \(\partial_t|E|^2\) is
\[
2(\nabla_p\nabla_q a)B_{\mathrm{def}}^{pq},
\qquad
B_{\mathrm{def}}
=
s\,g^{pq}+\tau E^{pq}-2(E^2)^{pq}.
\]
The sharp derivative estimate is
\[
|\nabla B_{\mathrm{def}}|
\le C|E||\nabla E|.
\]
The tensor is quadratic in \(E\), so the signed integration by parts preserves homogeneity and yields
\[
\varepsilon X_6+Cr^{-2}J_6
\]
rather than a curvature-only source [Step 35].

The normalization algebra was also repaired. The \(+g\) in \(E=\operatorname{Ric}+g\) produces no additional quadratic curvature term because of the skew symmetry \(R_{ijkl}+R_{ijlk}=0\). The lowering/inverse-metric variation gives the required scaling contribution. Under \(\partial_tg=-2g\),
\[
\partial_t|\operatorname{Rm}|^2=4|\operatorname{Rm}|^2,
\]
and \(\int|\operatorname{Rm}|^2d\mu\) is invariant in dimension four. The pre-absorption dissipation is
\[
-pD_p^{\mathrm{Rm}}-p(p-2)D_p^F,
\]
correcting the earlier \(p(p-3)\) statement [Steps 34–35].

These index identities and derivative structures brought the fixed-exponent curvature and defect energy modules to a tensor-level justified state, conditional on existence of the smooth fixed-cutoff flow and the provisional first-exit geometry. They did not by themselves prove the all-\(p\) flow theorem, continuation, or terminal smoothing [Step 35].

## Degenerate-flow platform, quantifier separation, and global \(Q\) [Step 36]

Step 36 shifted the main bottleneck from tensor algebra to the PDE platform. The Step 35 signed integration-by-parts formulas mean first smoothing estimates no longer depend on pointwise evolving cutoff-Hessian control. Higher cutoff jets remain a continuation issue, but they are no longer an input to the initial q=2, q=3, or \(J_6\) estimates [Steps 35–36].

Three quantifier levels were distinguished. Short-time smooth existence is required separately for each smooth closed datum; its lifespan may depend on the datum’s full geometry, including the frozen exterior. Sequence-uniform initial existence is unnecessary. Extension to the target time \(T=\theta r^2\) is a maximal-time issue: higher-derivative constants may depend on the individual datum and a positive starting time, but must stay finite as a hypothetical maximal endpoint is approached. By contrast, metric drift, terminal plateau curvature, Sobolev comparison, retained plateau volume, and global \(Q/A\) must be sequence-uniform for the geometric contradiction [Step 36].

The correct DeTurck formulation uses a transported coefficient
\[
\widehat a=a\circ\varphi_t^{-1}
\]
and the full gauge
\[
\mathcal L_{\widehat aW}\widehat g,
\]
not merely \(\widehat a\mathcal L_W\widehat g\). The product rule contributes the necessary \(d\widehat a\otimes W^\flat\) terms. With
\[
\partial_t\varphi_t\circ\varphi_t^{-1}=-\widehat aW,
\]
pullback recovers the fixed-cutoff normalized flow. The normalization perturbation linearizes as
\[
\delta(-2\widehat a\widehat g)
=
-2\widehat a\,h-2(\delta\widehat a)\widehat g.
\]
Yang’s tame transported-coefficient construction was accepted as the appropriate per-datum short-time model, with this lower-order normalized perturbation. A generic coefficient regularization \(a+\varepsilon\) was not ruled out in principle, but ordinary strictly parabolic Schauder estimates do not by themselves give the required \(\varepsilon\)-uniform fixed-datum limit [Step 36].

The unweighted global defect
\[
Q=\int_M|E|^2
\]
was isolated as an independent first-exit quantity. Neither \(J_6\) nor \(\|aE\|_\infty\) controls \(Q\) near the zero set of \(a\). On one buffered support \(U\), signed integration by parts and
\[
\frac{|da|^2}{a}=4|d\chi|^2
\]
give a homogeneous inequality of the form
\[
Q_U'+cX_U
\le
C(1+r^{-2})Q_U
+
C\int F(\chi E)^2.
\]
Because \(\eta=1\) on \(\operatorname{supp}\chi\), the buffered q=2 curvature energy and Sobolev inequality give
\[
\int F(\chi E)^2
\le
C\gamma(X_U+r^{-2}Q_U).
\]
For small \(\gamma\), the dissipation absorbs the potential. Summing over macro-disjoint active supports and using the stationary complement yields
\[
Q(t)\le e^{C(1+r^{-2})t}Q(0).
\]
At \(T=\theta r^2\), this is a sequence-uniform multiplicative factor and preserves \(Q(T)/A\to0\) [Step 36].

This global \(Q\) estimate is a genuine upstream-to-downstream bridge: it supplies the exact quantity needed for Step 28 terminal recalibration. It remains conditional on the smooth flow and first-exit support geometry, but it is logically independent of the later positive-time pointwise defect bound [Step 36].

## Shifted-curvature continuation: current role and remaining derivation [Steps 27–36]

The continuation variable remains
\[
T=\operatorname{Rm}+G,
\qquad
G=\frac{g\owedge g}{2(n-1)},
\qquad
U=aT.
\]
It satisfies
\[
\operatorname{Ric}(T)=E,\qquad
\operatorname{Ric}(U)=aE,
\]
so the flow velocity and connection variation can be written through \(U\), notably
\[
\partial_t\Gamma=g^{-1}*\nabla\operatorname{Ric}(U).
\]
This is the useful reason to keep \(U\); it is not a uniformly parabolic Moser substitute [Steps 27, 29–30, 36].

A03/Codex work developed a Wang-type staggered induction for \((\nabla^mU,\nabla^{m+1}\chi)\). Step 36’s cross-check accepted a signed Hessian-cutoff lemma: terms
\[
\int\chi\,\nabla_i\nabla_j\chi\,B^{ij}(V)
\]
with
\[
|B|\le C_p|V|^p,\qquad
|\nabla B|\le C_p|V|^{p-1}|\nabla V|
\]
can be integrated by parts once and handled by Young, rather than estimated through an uncontrolled pointwise \(\nabla^2\chi\). This repairs the finite-\(L^p\) base-pair layer and the apparent single-Hessian term at derivative level \(m=2\) [Step 36].

Continuation is not yet proved. The remaining work is to derive an unweighted finite-\(p\) energy inequality for \(T\) under \(\sup|U|<\infty\), write the complete index-level equations for \(U\) and \(W=\nabla U\) with every \(G\), normalization, connection, and cutoff term, and then complete the higher staggered induction without introducing coefficients such as \(\|T\|_\infty\), \(\|a\nabla\operatorname{Rm}\|_\infty\), or uncontrolled pointwise cutoff Hessians. A genuine next-derivative level and Sobolev embedding are then needed to obtain a smooth limit at a maximal endpoint [Step 36].

The key quantifier correction is that these higher derivative bounds need not be sequence-uniform. They may depend on the individual input and on a positive starting time; they only need to remain finite up to a putative maximal time. Sequence-uniformity is required instead for the lower-order first-exit estimates and terminal plateau geometry [Step 36].

## Selected-support construction and the current first-exit architecture [Steps 24–36]

The intended support family is not an all-centers maximal net. Maximal-function good centers must be assigned disjoint volume weights, outer-buffer interaction graphs must be colored, and one macro-disjoint color class must retain a fixed fraction of volume. The physical cutoffs have stationary outer collars, while the inner \(a=1\) plateaux must be large enough to contain all terminal exponential geodesics after metric comparison [Steps 24, 30].

A fixed retained volume fraction gives
\[
\operatorname{Vol}(P_i)\ge\alpha A_i
\]
only after combining it with the positive lower bound on \(\operatorname{Vol}(M_i)/A_i\). An upper volume bound alone does not suffice. Terminal eigenvalue or related calibration densities are to be zero-extended outside the bounded-curvature region before exponential-pullback averaging [Step 30].

The current simultaneous first-exit system has the following logical order:

1. per-datum short-time existence for the fixed-cutoff normalized flow via the transported DeTurck construction;
2. localized q=2 curvature energy \(K_2^\eta\), dissipation, and small critical parameter \(\gamma\);
3. integrated cubic potential \(B(t)=\int C_S^2Y\) and fixed q=3 good-slice/forward propagation;
4. high-\(p\) weighted Moser giving \(\|aF(t)\|_\infty\lesssim\gamma/t\) on positive-time slabs;
5. direct unregularized \(J_6\) persistence from time zero and subsequent defect Moser giving
   \[
   \|aE(t)\|_\infty\lesssim\delta(r^2/t)^{1/3};
   \]
6. integrable weighted velocity, yielding sequence-uniform metric and Sobolev comparison;
7. separate global \(Q(t)\lesssim Q(0)\) propagation;
8. shifted-\(U\) continuation to the common time \(T=\theta r^2\);
9. bounded-curvature inner plateaux with retained normalized mass;
10. terminal Seiberg–Witten/Chern–Weil recalibration, exponential-pullback selection, and the Derdziński contradiction [Steps 28, 30–36].

The tensor-level q=2/q=3 and \(J_6\) premises are now much stronger than at Step 27, and the global \(Q\) mechanism has been written. The decisive unresolved interface is proving smooth existence and shifted-\(U\) extension through the target time while closing the simultaneous first-exit inequalities. A bootstrap showing that lower-order bounds cannot fail does not by itself exclude termination of the smooth solution [Steps 35–36].

## Positive branch and higher-dimensional parallel work [Steps 5–36]

The positive branch remains strategically sufficient if a topology-independent forcing interval can be proved. Myers gives diameter control, and Bochner gives \(b_1=0\) and finite fundamental group under positive Ricci pinching. Bishop–Gromov gives no dimension-only volume lower bound; collapsing round lens-space quotients show that collapse can coexist with exact positive Einstein geometry [Steps 5–7].

S0910A02 developed four-dimensional toric, Kaluza–Klein, and spectral routes: orbit-area pinning, flux alternatives, edge and corner matching, Schrödinger/Faber–Krahn estimates, a noncollapsed dichotomy, and a possible obstruction involving \(\det R_+=0\). Local Kaluza–Klein jet tests showed that Ricci pinching need not control arbitrary local twist. A Bochner identity bounds brackets for a genuine central Killing field under positive Ricci upper control, but it does not control the full nonabelian action, horizontal O’Neill twist, or an almost-Killing collapse model [Steps 28–31].

The later positive collapsed-toric work corrected rod and period accounting. Conical singularities are period defects, finite noncompact alternating chains have an exact same-label period range, and compact-polygon period monodromy for \(m=6,8\) remains unresolved. The NUT-versus-strut and gravitational-instanton limits form a separate analytic front and do not supply evidence for the negative cutoff-flow theorem [Steps 34–36].

Higher-dimensional Kaluza–Klein examples show that codimension-one positive collapse can coexist with exact Einstein geometry in \(n\ge5\). Collapse alone is therefore not a positive obstruction. Although the critical analytic product
\[
r^2\left(\fint|\operatorname{Rm}|^{n/2}\right)^{2/n}
\]
has a dimension-independent form, the present Seiberg–Witten calibration, \(W^\pm\) decomposition, Derdziński germ, and Chern–Weil/Noether budget are intrinsically four-dimensional. No higher-dimensional replacement has been established [Steps 18–36].

## Current integrated position [Steps 1–36]

The durable restricted negative route developed as follows:

- Mixed Seiberg–Witten and Chern–Weil estimates reduced the principal LeBrun/Ishida–LeBrun candidate family to the full near-critical regime \(q/A\to0\), including sequences with \(q>0\) at every index [Steps 3–8, 29–30].
- Completion-square and tensor-gap estimates identified a calibrated Weyl profile, and Derdziński’s source-verified local theorem ruled out the resulting \(\operatorname{Ric}=-g\) Einstein germ [Steps 5–8].
- Cusp, Nil, Taub–NUT, orbit-volume, and Kaluza–Klein analyses showed that collapse and local nilpotent symmetry are not contradictions by themselves; what matters is access to controlled geometry carrying the normalized deficits [Steps 8–14].
- Noether and Chern–Weil provide only the needed \(O(A)\) curvature budget, not the later false asymptotic \(\chi=A+O(1)\) or \(K_0\to9\) [Steps 10–14, 29–30].
- Naive localized smoothing was corrected after finite-propagation, all-centers, Whitney-normalization, and graph-selection failures. The active construction uses selected macro-disjoint supports with stationary collars [Steps 14–25].
- Exponential pullback removed the downstream need for base noncollapse or Euler-density localization, provided the flow yields normalized plateau mass, bounded-curvature buffers, and \(Q(T)/A\to0\) [Steps 16–18, 28].
- The weighted Moser hierarchy survived several corrections: the half-power issue is repaired by mixed interpolation, unweighted \(U\)-Moser is withdrawn, the collapsed Sobolev coefficient is canceled by seed volume rather than made uniform, and the positive-time curvature and defect endpoints retain their \(t^{-1}\) and \(t^{-1/3}\) scalings [Steps 27–34].
- The q=3 integrated-potential/good-slice argument and direct unregularized \(J_6\) absorption sharply simplified the fixed-exponent layer [Step 34].
- Index-level Hessian-\(a\) contraction formulas established the signed integration-by-parts structure needed for both curvature and defect energies without pointwise cutoff-Hessian control [Step 35].
- The transported-coefficient DeTurck formulation clarified per-datum short-time existence, and a separate global \(Q\) estimate was built for terminal recalibration [Step 36].
- The remaining load-bearing analytic task is shifted-\(U\) continuation and simultaneous first-exit closure to a common target time, with lower-order outputs sequence-uniform but higher derivative extension allowed to depend on each individual datum [Step 36].

Several earlier “completion” or shortcut claims remain superseded: the Lohkamp counterexample, naive ALE scaling exclusion, Kähler blow-up construction, universal orbit-volume obstruction, Hessian semipositivity, finite-propagation localization, Whitney-volume-normal energy inheritance, all-exponent critical absorption, unweighted \(U\)-Moser, collapse-independent unnormalized Dirichlet Sobolev constants, \(\chi=A+O(1)\), \(K_0\to9\), time-uniform Moser endpoints, and pointwise evolving cutoff-Hessian input for first smoothing are all withdrawn or replaced by the current structure [Steps 1–36].

No complete theorem for the original Yau Problem 26, or even for the full four-dimensional negative branch, has yet been proved. Completion of the current analytic platform would yield a substantial defect-gap result only for the near-critical Ishida–LeBrun negative laboratory. The positive branch, arbitrary four-dimensional topology, dimensions \(n\ge5\), dimension-only interval constants, and Lean formalization remain open [Steps 1–36].

### Decisions and Recorded Reasons

- The research goal remains unchanged: for every \(n\ge2\), prove or refute the existence of dimension-only constants \(c_n<C_n\) such that every closed connected smooth \(n\)-manifold carrying a metric with
  \[
  c_ng\le \operatorname{Ric}_g\le C_ng
  \]
  also carries some Einstein metric. Ultimate completion still requires a reproducible Lean 4 proof and independent kernel and axiom audit. No sign branch or unresolved dimension has been settled [Steps 1–36].

- The normalized sign-branch logic remains basic: proving either a sufficiently tight positive or sufficiently tight negative branch in each dimension would establish the interval proposition. Refuting it requires defeating both possible sign choices in the same dimension. The early accidental demand to prove both branches was corrected [Steps 1, 3].

- Dimension three remains a classical baseline rather than the main investment: \(W=0\), tight Ricci pinching controls sectional curvature, and Hamilton’s positive-Ricci theorem supplies the positive branch. The research therefore concentrated on unresolved higher-dimensional mechanisms [Steps 2–3].

- Four-dimensional LeBrun/Ishida–LeBrun connected sums remain the principal negative obstruction laboratory. They provide smooth closed manifolds carrying no Einstein metric of any sign, including examples beyond the elementary Hitchin–Thorpe obstruction. They remain only a laboratory: no-Einstein topology does not itself produce a tightly two-sided Ricci-pinched metric [Steps 1–4].

- Lohkamp’s work remains classified as one-sided negative-Ricci flexibility, not two-sided near-Einstein flexibility. Min–Oo-type stability results remain insufficient without extra diameter, sectional-curvature, or bounded-geometry hypotheses because a near-pinched sequence could collapse, concentrate curvature, or develop large diameter [Steps 1–2].

- The negative laboratory was narrowed from the scalar Seiberg–Witten estimate to the mixed estimate
  \[
  \frac1{4\pi^2}\int\left(\frac{s^2}{24}+2|W^+|^2\right)\ge\frac23(a^+)^2.
  \]
  For the connected-sum parameters, the relevant difficult regime is \(q=k-A/3\to0\), not the earlier scalar-only \(A^{-1/2}\) opening. This is where the current curvature budget loses a uniform margin, not an established Einstein-existence boundary [Steps 3–4].

- Direct Kähler blow-up and Arezzo–Pacard constructions were removed as uniformly negative-Ricci candidates because exceptional curves conflict with that negativity. Corrected ALE gluing remains logically open: a relative \(O(t^2)\) correction on a core scaled by \(t^2\) can have order-one normalized Ricci effect. Taub–Bolt–AdS showed that exceptional topology alone need not create a cap error; interface data and the gauge-fixed linear matching problem are the relevant issues [Steps 3–4].

- The principal negative route shifted from cap optimization to quantitative stability of LeBrun equality. With
  \[
  I=\frac1{4\pi^2}\int\left(\frac{s^2}{24}+2|W^+|^2\right),\qquad
  J=\frac1{4\pi^2}\int\frac{|\operatorname{Ric}^{\circ}|^2}{2},
  \]
  and \(D_a=I-\frac23(a^+)^2\),
  \[
  D_a=J-q-\frac23\big((a^+)^2-A\big),\qquad 0\le D_a\le J-q.
  \]
  This exact relation made equality stability, rather than direct metric construction, the central theoretical issue [Step 4].

- Chern–Gauss–Bonnet was adopted for volume and curvature-budget control. The completion-square remainder became the principal calibration:
  \[

  This Weyl norm is incompatible with a negative Kähler–Einstein exterior, so the proposed architecture of a macroscopically Kähler–Einstein background plus negligible-volume topological insertions was rejected [Steps 5–6].

- Global compactness claims were deliberately weakened. Since topology, volume, diameter, and scale may vary, a normalized small deficit does not force absolute pointwise saturation on every region. Collapse, concentration, spatial escape, and bounded-volume islands remain possible. The geometric target became a positive normalized volume of selected fixed-scale regions rather than global convergence [Steps 6–8].

- Derdziński’s local theorem remains the forbidden-germ mechanism. At the calibrated double eigenvalue, a smooth Einstein limit would be locally conformally Kähler; the calibrated value \(|W^+|^2=1/24\) conflicts with the negative Kähler–Einstein identity \(|W^+|^2=s^2/24=2/3\) when \(s=-4\). The contradiction is through local conformal Kählerity plus the modulus conflict, not through an eigenframe-dependent assertion such as \(\nabla W^+=0\). Scalar modulus control alone is insufficient; a tensor spectral-gap deficit must also vanish [Steps 7–8, 29].

Bounded Ricci, \(C^{1,\alpha}\) metric convergence, and harmonic-coordinate ellipticity are intended to give strong curvature convergence on smaller charts; only the limiting weak Einstein metric is bootstrapped smoothly [Steps 7–8].

## Four-dimensional topology candidates and construction bottlenecks [Steps 1–5]

The principal all-sign Einstein-obstructed candidates became LeBrun/Ishida–LeBrun blow-ups

where \(X\) is a minimal complex surface of general type and \(A=c_1^2(X)\). Elementary equality or violating families already have Chern–Weil gaps against arbitrarily tight Ricci pinching and are poor candidates for a vanishing-defect sequence [Steps 1–2].

Connected-sum arithmetic was repaired:

\tau=m,\qquad
2\chi-3\tau=4-m.
\]
Thus \(m=4\) is the equality case, \(m\ge5\) violates Hitchin–Thorpe, and \(m=3\) does not. Later positive-branch candidate discussions were required to respect this correction [Steps 3–4].

Positive-Ricci constructions of Reiser, Burdick, and related core-metric work showed that many connected sums carry \(\operatorname{Ric}>0\), but no verified family combined an all-sign Einstein obstruction, strict Hitchin–Thorpe compatibility, and metrics with arbitrarily small positive Einstein defect. A later correction prevented this from becoming a false exclusion: an \(O(t^2)\) relative correction to a \(t^2\)-scaled Ricci-flat core can itself produce order-one Ricci curvature. Corrected gluing is therefore a linearized solvability and Cauchy-data matching problem. A straightforward Kähler blow-up route was excluded. Arezzo–Pacard-style and other Kähler constructions therefore cannot realize the desired sequence; any surviving construction must be genuinely non-Kähler [Steps 3–4].
