It recovered the static relation \(\operatorname{Spec}(W^+)=\{1/3-\eta_i\}\) and corrected the mixed equation to
\[
\operatorname{div}(v^3F)=0.
\]
A curvature sign convention in the script’s `Ric[33]` output was noted for repair [Step 13].

An attempted bootstrap claimed that calibrated \(W^+\) forced a semipositive Hessian \(H\). This was withdrawn. The exact identity
\[
H=\frac13I+T(z)-\frac12(W^++W^-),\qquad
T(z)=\frac14\big(|z|^2I-z\otimes z\big)\ge0
\]
leaves anti-self-dual curvature free. If \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\le-\eta\), then
\[
\lambda_{\max}(W^-)\ge\frac7{12}+2\eta,
\]
with an order-one \(W^-\)-energy cost. A compatible first-order Kaluza–Klein jet and the example \(H^2\times H^2\) disprove “static implies \(H\ge0\)” [Step 13].

The chiral factorization
\[
W^\pm=-[\operatorname{sym}\nabla a_\pm+a_\pm\otimes a_\pm]_0,\qquad
da_+=a_+\wedge a_-
\]
organized the remaining local data but did not close reconstruction. It exposed five uncontrolled anti-self-dual/derivative-twist components and trace modes. Even Hessian positivity would still leave base collapse, absolute volume anchoring, lower bounds for \(v\), fiber homotopy survival, and reconstruction unresolved [Steps 13–14].

## Fixed-scale smoothing and the false localization completion [Steps 14–16]

Ye Li’s four-dimensional smoothing theorem was revisited. An earlier objection that the calibrated nonzero background curvature prevents small-energy smoothing was incorrect. Li’s hypothesis is the dimensionless condition
\[
r^4\fint_{B_r(x)}|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\le\varepsilon_{\rm Li}.
\]
On maximal-function good sets, the Chern–Weil/Noether budget gives a uniform local mean \(K_0\). Choosing a sufficiently small but fixed physical radius \(r_*\), before taking the sequence limit, makes \(K_0r_*^4\) small while preserving the nonzero \(\operatorname{Ric}\approx-g\) scale [Step 14]. This shifted the main geometric bridge from collapse classification to fixed-small-scale smoothing.

Li’s stated theorem is complete and all-centers, not a selected-ball local theorem. A good center controls only a comparable buffer. Other local-flow sources require noncollapse, Sobolev control, GH models, or maximal nilpotency. The promising four-dimensional calculation was the collapse-independent critical product
\[
A_R\lesssim\frac{R^2}{\operatorname{Vol}(B_R)^{1/2}},\qquad
\|\operatorname{Rm}\|_{L^2(B_R)}
\lesssim\sqrt{K_0\operatorname{Vol}(B_R)},
\]
so
\[
A_R\|\operatorname{Rm}\|_{L^2(B_R)}
\lesssim R^2\sqrt{K_0}.
\]
This suggested that curvature-reaction terms could be absorbed even while the Sobolev coefficient diverges under collapse [Steps 14–15].

Step 15 assembled a cutoff flow
\[
\partial_tg=-2\chi^2(\operatorname{Ric}+g)
\]
using maximal-function good sets, Vitali-separated supports, plateau regions, the homogeneity of \(E=\operatorname{Ric}+g\), and topological recalibration after smoothing. Because the smoothed metric remains on the same closed manifold, the mixed Seiberg–Witten and Chern–Weil inequalities can be rerun rather than transporting \(W^+\) through the flow. A completion-square calculation from S0910A03 supported regeneration of the calibrated modulus from a small terminal \(L^2\) Einstein defect; the existing Step 8 density \(G\) remained the correct spectral passage [Steps 15–16].

Step 15 nevertheless declared the smoothing chain complete on invalid grounds. Step 16 found two decisive quantifier failures. Ricci flow has no finite propagation speed, so a plateau wider than \(\sqrt t\) does not isolate its interior from transition geometry. Li’s bootstrap supremum also ranges over all centers in the working region; estimating only an inner center set while covering balls reach a larger set leaves an unclosed inner/outer inequality. Agreement across sessions based on the same localization argument was not independent confirmation [Steps 15–16].

The completion claim was withdrawn in `notes/step15_cutoff_smoothing_architecture.md` and `plans/route_assessment_step15.md`. The repaired theorem target became transition-inclusive: prove metric comparability, Sobolev persistence, curvature-energy persistence, interior smoothing, and
\[
Q_i(t)/A_i\to0,\qquad Q_i(t)=\int|E_i(t)|^2,
\]
with all cutoff derivative terms retained. Homogeneity removes additive forcing when \(E=0\), but does not by itself bound amplification of a small nonzero defect [Step 16].

A proposed harmonic-form/eigenline shortcut was also rejected. A global harmonic form may vanish on every selected chart, and the harmonic representative of a monopole class cannot simply be identified with the self-dual form in the Seiberg–Witten proof. Unique continuation does not provide a uniform local mass bound. The completion-square modulus and explicit tensor deficit \(G\) were restored as the direct spectral mechanism [Step 16].

## Exponential-pullback averaging and the post-smoothing architecture [Steps 16–18]

Once bounded-sectional-curvature buffers are available, exponential pullback can bypass much of the normal-cover rank classification. Rauch Jacobian comparison and Liouville invariance of geodesic flow transfer small mean nonnegative deficit densities from the base to controlled tangent-space pullback balls. Averaging can then select a chart with small Einstein, scalar, and tensor-calibration deficits without proving that a short nilpotent orbit survives in a local fundamental group [Steps 16–17].

This mechanism is conditional on positive-volume bounded-curvature plateaux, but downstream it avoids reopening abelian/Nil rank tables, CFG maximal-rank hypotheses, contractible-fiber questions, and normal-cover reconstruction solely for the local contradiction. The pulled-back metric need not be globally injective. Uniform terminal curvature plus vanishing local \(L^2\) Einstein defect gives finite-\(p\) convergence; harmonic-coordinate elliptic regularity then produces a smooth Einstein limit carrying the calibrated deficits [Steps 16–17].

Support geometry was made consistent at a fixed ratio of one small scale: Vitali selection, separated centers, supports, plateaux, and smaller bootstrap regions. Comparable-ball Bishop–Gromov transfer preserved
\[
r_*^4\fint_{B_{r_*}(y)}|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\le CK_0r_*^4
\]
and the critical Sobolev product. A residual claim that enlarging the plateau completed Li’s bootstrap was removed in Step 18: static containment of covering balls does not close an evolving center supremum [Steps 17–18].

Step 18 recast the remaining problem as a degenerate parabolic system. With
\[
a=\chi^2,\qquad E=\operatorname{Ric}+g,\qquad
\partial_tg=-2aE,
\]
weighted curvature \(a\operatorname{Rm}\), weighted velocity \(aE\), and unweighted \(Q=\int|E|^2\) have distinct roles. A bound on \(aE\) does not control \(Q\) where \(a\to0\), so normalized unweighted defect preservation must be proved separately [Step 18].

For a scalar curvature magnitude \(K\), setting \(f=aK\) changes the quadratic reaction to \(cf^2\), not \(cf^2/a\), while
\[
\frac{|\nabla a|^2}{a}=4|\nabla\chi|^2.
\]
Integrated scalar algebra cancels a \(\Delta a\) term by parts, suggesting that pointwise Hessian bounds for \(\chi\) might be avoidable. The full tensor equation still contains \(\nabla^2a*E*\operatorname{Rm}\), \(\nabla a*\nabla E*\operatorname{Rm}\), moving metric and volume, and changing Sobolev geometry. This became the load-bearing analytic frontier [Step 18].

## Whitney localization and the correction of multiscale energy claims [Steps 19–22]

Step 19 concentrated on the Whitney representation of the cutoff degeneracy. Near a point where \(\chi=\chi_0>0\), take a ball of radius
\[
\ell=cr\chi_0.
\]
On this ball \(a/a_0\), \(a_0=\chi_0^2\), has a uniformly bounded ellipticity ratio. Physical time of order \(r^2\) corresponds to a fixed rescaled diffusion time because both the diffusion coefficient and \(\ell^2\) carry \(\chi_0^2\). Bishop–Gromov transfer from a support-total energy budget gives
\[
\ell^4\fint_{B_\ell}|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\lesssim K_0r^4,
\]
and the four-dimensional Sobolev reaction product remains independent of \(\chi_0\) and collapsed volume [Step 19]. The cancellations were explored in `notes/step19_whitney_tensor_estimate.md` and scripts including `step19_whitney_energy_transfer.py` and `step19_tensor_whitney_absorption.py`.

The tensor structure was sharpened in Step 20. Since \(E=\operatorname{Ric}+g\), current Levi-Civita compatibility gives \(\nabla E=\operatorname{contr}(\nabla\operatorname{Rm})\). After integrating \(\nabla^2a\) terms by parts, the \(\nabla E\) factors can in principle be absorbed into the full tensor curvature dissipation, with remaining cutoff terms carrying the regular coefficient \(|da|^2/a\). This replaced an unnecessarily independent high-power curvature–defect system by a curvature-power estimate plus a separate unweighted defect estimate [Step 20].

The direct all-exponent critical absorption suggested in Step 19 was not justified: coefficients grow with the power \(q\), so a fixed critical threshold can be exhausted. The route changed to finite exponents—\(q=2\), parabolic Sobolev, \(q=3\)—followed by a positive-time subcritical Moser argument. A separate correction rejected any defect estimate with an additive \(\varepsilon X\) curvature-dissipation remainder: if \(\int X=O(A)\), this leaves \(O(\varepsilon A)\), not \(o(A)\). The required defect equation is triangular, with curvature acting as a potential multiplying \(E^2\) and no curvature-only source [Step 20].

Step 21 built a conditional finite-exponent chain, but a scaling error was found in its terminal Stampacchia step. Under \(\tilde g=\ell^{-2}g\),
\[
|\operatorname{Rm}(\tilde g)|=\ell^2|\operatorname{Rm}(g)|,
\]
so the raw rescaled estimate gives only \(\ell^2F\le C\), not a scale-free bound for \(F\). This was replaced by a weighted \(q\mapsto3q/2\) Moser product. The weaker bound \(a|\operatorname{Rm}|\lesssim r^{-2}\) was recognized as potentially sufficient for bounded-curvature plateau geometry at the fixed chosen scale; a sharper small factor is needed only where stability or velocity absorption uses it [Step 21].

Step 22 uncovered a more fundamental normalization error. If a support \(U\) satisfies
\[
\int_UF^2\le M\operatorname{Vol}(U),
\]
a smaller Whitney ball \(W=B_\ell(y)\) need not satisfy the same volume-normalized mean. Nonconcentric Bishop–Gromov comparison only gives
\[
\operatorname{Vol}(W)\gtrsim(\ell/r)^4\operatorname{Vol}(U),
\]
so \(\fint_WF^2\) can grow like \((r/\ell)^4\). The valid invariant quantities are
\[
\ell^4\fint_WF^2
\quad\text{and}\quad
A_W^2\|F\|_{L^2(W)},
\]
not a uniform Whitney-volume-normal \(L^2\) bound. This forced the analysis to keep component energy, relative Sobolev coefficient, and weighted moments distinct [Step 22]. It also removed the incorrect inference that small metric displacement keeps transition curvature close to its initial value.

A graph formulation using \(S_\alpha=A_\alpha^4H_{2,\alpha}\) and nested weighted moments was developed to preserve these normalizations. Verification identified the need for outer cutoffs, correctly shrinking time intervals, and graph-semigroup rather than fixed-neighbor propagation. The weighted moment ledger used
\[
H_q=\int\eta^2a^{q-2}F^q,\qquad
v_q=\eta a^{(q-1)/2}F^{q/2},
\]
and an outer cubic moment; the same-cutoff identity previously used for \(H_{2q}\) was false [Step 22].

## Conditional graph persistence and return to selected good supports [Steps 23–24]

Step 23 addressed a formal localization problem in the graph system. Summing neighbor dissipations gives total energy control but not a componentwise critical bound. A positive resolvent
\[
P=(I-\rho B)^{-1}
\]
for a bounded neighbor matrix \(B\) was proposed to absorb neighbor dissipation while retaining localized weighted sums. More importantly, examination of the Sobolev variable
\[
v_\alpha=\eta_\alpha a^{1/2}F
\]
showed that its gradient terms are supported in the same energy domain. The Sobolev absorption therefore uses the same component’s dissipation, not neighbor dissipations. A maximal \(r\)-net with subordinate cutoffs repaired the formal coverage identity, and a cooperative system could conditionally propagate componentwise \(H_2\), integrated dissipation, cubic moments, \(Q\), and fixed \(J_6\) [Step 23].

This apparent closure did not match the actual LeBrun sequence. A maximal net over all of \(M\) includes centers outside the maximal-function good set, while the global curvature budget does not make the critical product small at every center. Step 24 therefore retained the cooperative graph theorem only as an all-centers conditional result. It cannot replace the selected-good-support construction [Step 24].

The active formulation returned to individually selected buffered supports. On each support choose the physical cutoff \(\chi\) with its full transition region compactly contained in a domain where an auxiliary energy cutoff \(\eta=1\), and place \(\operatorname{supp}\nabla\eta\) in an open collar where \(\chi=0\). Then
\[
a|\nabla\eta|^2=0,\qquad \nabla a\cdot\nabla\eta=0,
\]
and the collar is exactly stationary because the flow coefficient vanishes there. This is a support identity, not a finite-propagation assertion. All active transition terms remain inside the energy domain [Step 24].

At a selected good center, the whole auxiliary support has controlled initial \(L^2\) curvature and relative Sobolev coefficient, giving
\[
\beta_0=A_\Omega^2H_2(0)^{1/2}
\lesssim r^2\sqrt{1+K_0}
\]
with collapsed volume cancelling. The scale \(r\) must be chosen after support ratios and tensor constants; illustrative scripts showed that an inherited numerical choice could be too large and then computed a smaller admissible sample scale [Step 24].

The proposed support-local q=2 inequality became
\[
H_2'+cD_2
\le C\int aF^3+Cr^{-2}H_2.
\]
The reaction is tested by \(\chi F\), remains in the selected support, and is absorbable through the active critical parameter
\[
\beta_a(t)=A_\Omega^2\|F(t)\|_{L^2(\operatorname{supp}\chi)}.
\]
Its time integral supplies the correctly weighted cubic moment \(\int\!\!\int aF^3\) [Step 24].

For q=3, a first Riccati-style argument was rejected. The correct Sobolev variable is
\[
u=aF^{3/2},
\]
not \(\chi F^{3/2}\). If
\[
Y=\int\eta^2aF^3,\qquad
D_3=\int\eta^2a^2F|\nabla\operatorname{Rm}|^2,
\]
then
\[
\int a^2F^4
\lesssim\beta_a(D_3+r^{-2}Y).
\]
Time averaging followed by linear propagation can conditionally give \(A_\Omega^4Y(t)\lesssim\beta^3/t\). The weighted \(aF^3\) moment was explicitly distinguished from the \(a^{3/2}F^3\) produced by a naive parabolic Sobolev application [Step 24].

A static packing and coloring argument showed that disjoint selected supports can retain a positive sequence-independent plateau volume fraction, although the crude constant may be extremely small. Such a fixed fraction is enough for later normalized averaging if the PDE estimates provide bounded-curvature plateaux [Step 24].

## Tensor energy derivation and global defect bookkeeping [Step 25]

Step 25 derived the buffered-support tensor inequalities at a schematic but substantially checked level. Under
\[
\partial_tg=-2aE,\qquad a=\chi^2,\qquad E=\operatorname{Ric}+g,
\]
the q=2 curvature calculation classified the variation into the principal Bochner term, first-derivative cutoff terms, Hessian-\(a\) terms, algebraic curvature coupling, moving inverse metric, and moving volume. Integrating Hessian-\(a\) by parts and using
\[
\nabla^2a=2\,d\chi\otimes d\chi+2\chi\nabla^2\chi,\qquad
|da|^2/a=4|d\chi|^2
\]
reduces the transition terms to tensor dissipation, curvature reaction, and \(r^{-2}H_2\) localization terms. The buffered support removes cross terms involving \(\nabla\eta\) [Step 25]. The derivation and algebraic checks are in `notes/step25_tensor_energy_derivation.md` and `scripts/step25_tensor_energy_verification.py`.

The normalized \(-2ag\) part does not give free coercive curvature damping. The \(-2aR_{ijkl}\) tensor contribution is canceled in the norm variation by the inverse-metric terms. The calibration is the pure conformal flow \(g(t)=e^{-2t}g_0\), for which \(|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\) grows as \(e^{4t}\) and \(d\mu\) shrinks as \(e^{-4t}\), leaving \(\int|\operatorname{Rm}|^2d\mu\) constant. For \(F^2=1+|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\), only a bounded volume source remains; previous damping language was withdrawn [Step 25].

The defect equation was organized in triangular form:
\[
Q'+cX\le Cr^{-2}Q+C\int aF|E|^2.
\]
Because the flow velocity vanishes when \(E=0\), no independent curvature-only or Hessian-\(a\) forcing can remain after Ricci variation and normalization are combined. The potential is intended to be absorbed using \(\chi E\) and the same critical curvature product [Steps 24–25].

The selected-support formulation also simplified global defect preservation. If the auxiliary supports are disjoint, \(\eta_j=1\) on every physical flow support, and the complement is stationary, then
\[
Q_{\rm global}(t)-Q_{\rm global}(0)
=
\sum_j\big(Q_j(t)-Q_j(0)\big).
\]
A uniform multiplicative support estimate \(Q_j(t)\le C Q_j(0)\) gives
\[
Q_{\rm global}(t)\le\max\{1,C\}Q_{\rm global}(0)
\]
independently of the number of supports. Initial pinching gives \(Q_{\rm global}(0)\lesssim\delta^2\operatorname{Vol}(g_0)\), hence \(Q_{\rm global}(t)/A\to0\) using the established volume bound. No additional defect selection is needed on the frozen bad-curvature complement [Step 25].

An initial first-exit proposal tried to use short-time existence from the \(L^2\) good-center bound; this was rejected because local existence time depends on uncontrolled pointwise curvature peaks. A second claim that plateau regularity alone controlled transition displacement was also later withdrawn. The exact tensor derivation remained useful, but uniform continuation still required support-wide weighted curvature and weighted velocity [Steps 25–26].

A Codex worker begun in Step 24 completed `workspace/codex_loop/Research_Report.md` and `workspace/codex_loop/work/tensor_energy_derivation.md`. Its independent derivation confirmed the q=2 curvature, weighted q=3 curvature, and triangular defect weight structure, while also emphasizing the missing metric-comparison bootstrap. The output was treated as supporting analysis rather than unverified proof [Step 26].

## Support-wide weighted velocity and local-flow sources [Step 26]

Step 26 restored the transition stability target
\[
V(t)=\int_0^t\|aE(s)\|_{L^\infty(\operatorname{supp}\chi)}\,ds.
\]
Metric comparison on the full active support is
\[
e^{-2V(t)}g_0\le g(t)\le e^{2V(t)}g_0.
\]
The small factor \(a(x)\) does not automatically protect a transition point because \(E\) may grow as \(a\) decreases. Plateau curvature control is sufficient only for terminal geometry, not for preserving the Sobolev and energy environment during the flow [Step 26].

The useful new object was the fixed-power defect energy
\[
J_p=\int\eta^2a^{p-2}|E|^p.
\]
Its dissipation is
\[
Z_p=\int\eta^2a^{p-1}|E|^{p-2}|\nabla E|^2.
\]
The transition remainder uses
\[
a^{p-3}|da|^2|E|^p
=
4|d\chi|^2a^{p-2}|E|^p,
\]
and the curvature potential factors through
\[
z_p=\eta a^{(p-1)/2}|E|^{p/2},\qquad
\int Fz_p^2.
\]
Thus the same support critical curvature product can absorb the potential. The initial near-Einstein pointwise bound gives \(J_p(0)\lesssim\delta^p\operatorname{Vol}(\Omega)\) without high-power assumptions on full curvature [Step 26].

The choice \(p=6\) matches the four-dimensional weighted iteration:
\[
J_6=\int\eta^2\chi^8|E|^6,\qquad
Z_6=\int\eta^2\chi^{10}|E|^4|\nabla E|^2.
\]
The non-smooth factor \(|E|^3\) at \(E=0\) must be handled by weak Kato or \((|E|^2+\varepsilon)^{3/2}\) regularization, not assumed smooth. The exponent ledger was checked in `scripts/step26_fixed_p_defect_velocity.py` and `scripts/step26_p6_defect_energy_ledger.py` [Step 26].

Yang’s local Ricci-flow source was then read directly. Its DeTurck construction transports the cutoff coefficient as \((\chi\circ\phi^{-1})^2\) in the hatted equation; pulling back recovers the fixed spatial coefficient \(\chi^2\). For the normalized flow, the lower-order term \(-2(\chi\circ\phi^{-1})^2\hat g\) must be included as well. This resolved the concern that a naive gauge-fixed construction might solve a different transported-cutoff equation [Step 26].

Yang’s uniform-time theorem is itself a first-exit theorem controlling Sobolev geometry, metric comparison, current curvature energy, and weighted pointwise curvature. Wang’s extension mechanism requires support-wide control of \(|\chi^2\operatorname{Rm}|\). Thus short-time existence for each smooth input is only a starting point; the research needs a common time \(\theta r^2\) under simultaneous weighted curvature and velocity estimates [Step 26].

Yang Appendix B showed a striking weight match: in dimension four with \(p_0=q=6\), the input for \(f=|E|\) is \(\chi^8|E|^6\), and the curvature potential uses \((\int\chi^2F^3)^{1/3}\). Formal scaling gives
\[
\|aE(t)\|_\infty
\lesssim
\delta\left(\frac{r^2}{t}\right)^{1/3},
\]
whose time integral is \(O(\delta r^2\theta^{2/3})\). Direct invocation of Yang’s scalar theorem was not yet justified because the tensor Hessian-\(a\) contractions do not reduce pointwise to its scalar \(\chi\Delta\chi\) structure. The source was therefore retained as an iteration template rather than a black-box theorem [Steps 26–27].

## Unified weak Moser hierarchy and normalized continuation framework [Step 27]

Step 27 replaced direct scalar reduction by a common weak tensor iteration. Let
\[
Y=\int aF^3,\qquad
H_p(f)=\int a^{p-2}f^p,\qquad
z_p=a^{(p-1)/2}f^{p/2},
\]
on the physical support where the auxiliary cutoff is one. The central three-factor identity is
\[
a^{p-1}Ff^p
=
(aF^3)^{1/3}
(a^{p-2}f^p)^{1/3}
z_p^{4/3}.
\]
Hölder with exponents \((3,3,3)\), Sobolev, and Young convert the curvature reaction into an arbitrarily small multiple of \(\|\nabla z_p\|_2^2\) plus a lower-order coefficient of order \(S^2Y\) multiplying \(H_p\), where \(S\) is the squared relative Sobolev coefficient. This avoids critical absorption at every exponent: the positive-time cubic potential is a linear Gronwall coefficient, and polynomial \(p\)-growth is compatible with a convergent Moser product [Step 27]. The algebra and volume cancellations are recorded in `notes/step27_unified_weak_moser_iteration.md` and `scripts/step27_three_factor_absorption.py`.

The same hierarchy has two different seeds:

- For curvature, take \(f=F\) and \(p_0=3\), so \(H_3(F)=Y\). If the q=2/q=3 chain supplies \(S^2Y(s)\lesssim\beta^3/s\) on a positive-time slab, the Moser prefactor and seed cancel the Sobolev powers, formally giving
  \[
  \|aF(t)\|_\infty\lesssim\frac{\beta}{t}.
  \]
- For defect, take \(f=|E|\) and \(p_0=6\), with \(J_6\lesssim\delta^6\operatorname{Vol}(\Omega)\). The seed volume cancels the relative Sobolev volume factor, formally giving
  \[
  \|aE(t)\|_\infty
  \lesssim
  \delta\left(\frac{r^2}{t}\right)^{1/3}.
  \]

These are conditional consequences of the weak power inequalities and positive-time cubic estimate, not yet independently completed pointwise theorems [Step 27].

For continuation, a naive \(\varepsilon\)-regularization of the degenerate operator was withdrawn because sequence-uniform higher estimates were unavailable. The preferred formulation uses the shifted curvature
\[
T=\operatorname{Rm}+G,\qquad
G=\frac{g\owedge g}{2(n-1)},
\]
so \(\operatorname{Ric}(T)=E\) and \(\nabla G=0\). The weighted tensor \(U=aT\) is intended to satisfy the same structural local-flow equation used by Wang. A joint induction on \((\nabla^mU,\nabla^{m+1}\chi)\) is needed because high derivatives of the evolving cutoff coefficient involve cutoff jets; they cannot be hidden in a generic lower-order constant. `notes/step27_normalized_continuation_theorem.md` and the parallel A03 note formulate this normalized DeTurck/Yang/Wang adaptation [Step 27].

The current proposed first-exit package is therefore simultaneous rather than sequential:

1. selected-support q=2 curvature energy persistence and integrated dissipation;
2. the correctly weighted q=3 positive-time cubic potential;
3. fixed \(J_6\) defect persistence with no curvature-only source;
4. unified weak Moser outputs for support-wide \(aF\) and \(aE\);
5. integrable weighted velocity, preserving metric and Sobolev comparability;
6. shifted-curvature extension to the common time \(\theta r^2\).

The algebraic cancellations and source matching are strong, but the complete tensor power hierarchy, first-exit closure, and normalized extension theorem remain to be written and independently verified as one rigorous proof [Steps 25–27].

## Terminal recalibration and the newly isolated plateau-access problem [Step 27]

After a successful flow, the calibrated deficits must not be transported by \(C^0\) comparison. The correct order is to use the global defect identity to obtain
\[
Q_{\rm global}(T)/A\to0,
\]
then reapply the mixed Seiberg–Witten inequality, Chern–Gauss–Bonnet, and Step 8 completion-square/tensor-gap inequalities directly to the terminal closed metric on the same smooth manifold. Because the inequalities are topological and metric-universal, this should regenerate the scalar, Weyl-modulus, and eigenvalue deficits on \(g(T)\). A fixed positive terminal plateau fraction is then enough to make their normalized means vanish there. This terminal recalibration is structurally correct but still needs a complete chain checking volume normalization and every terminal hypothesis [Steps 25, 27].

A further downstream issue was isolated at Step 27. Bounded curvature on selected plateaux does not automatically give noncollapse or a smooth base-manifold chart. Two candidate bridges remain:

- use Euler-characteristic growth together with Cheeger–Gromov/F-structure theory to show that fully collapsed bounded-curvature plateaux cannot carry all relevant topology;
- use the exponential-pullback averaging mechanism from Steps 16–18 to extract controlled tangent-space charts without assuming quotient noncollapse.

Either route must ensure that an accessible controlled region intersects the positive-volume selected plateaux and carries vanishing terminal Einstein and calibrated tensor deficits. The proposed Euler argument was not proved; fully collapsed bounded-curvature topology and localization of Euler density require quantitative treatment. Exponential pullback remains the more developed local mechanism, but its terminal density selection has not yet been written as a complete theorem [Step 27].

If this plateau-access problem is solved, a controlled local sequence with vanishing Einstein defect and terminal scalar/tensor deficits should converge to the forbidden calibrated Einstein germ, giving the Derdziński contradiction. Even that would establish only a defect gap for the critical LeBrun/Ishida–LeBrun negative laboratory, not the full negative branch [Step 27].

## Positive branch and higher-dimensional parallel work [Steps 5–27]

The positive branch remains strategically sufficient if a topology-independent forcing interval can be proved, but no general mechanism has emerged. Myers supplies diameter control under positive pinching; Bochner gives \(b_1=0\) and finite fundamental group. Bishop–Gromov gives a volume upper bound, not a dimension-only lower bound, and collapsing round lens-space quotients show that collapse can coexist with exact positive Einstein geometry [Steps 5–7].

Cheeger–Naber noncollapsed finiteness does not provide noncollapse or Einstein existence. Four-dimensional toric work in S0910A02 developed Schrödinger/Faber–Krahn estimates, orbit-area pinning, flux alternatives, edge-germ compatibility, and later corner matching, but only in symmetry-reduced models. The toric integral route reached a “break” assessment: the available integral identities do not by themselves obstruct tight positive pinching on connected sums such as \(\#_k(S^2\times S^2)\) [Steps 9–27].

Naive positive counterexamples based on Hitchin–Thorpe violators were corrected because sufficiently tight pinching itself enforces strict Hitchin–Thorpe. A viable family must remain strictly compatible and carry metrics approaching the unknown threshold. Positive Ricci existence is insufficient [Steps 17–18].

Higher-dimensional Kaluza–Klein examples investigated by S0910A02 show that codimension-one positive collapse can be compatible with exact Einstein geometry in \(n\ge5\). Collapse alone is therefore not a positive-branch obstruction. The Sobolev-critical product
\[
r^2\left(\fint|\operatorname{Rm}|^{n/2}\right)^{2/n}
\]
is dimension-independent in form, so a successful defect-preserving smoothing theorem may have reusable analytic content. The present Seiberg–Witten calibration, \(W^\pm\) decomposition, Derdziński germ, and Chern–Weil/Noether budget are intrinsically four-dimensional, and no higher-dimensional replacement has been established [Steps 18–27].

## Current integrated position [Steps 1–27]

The durable four-dimensional negative route now has the following development:

- mixed Seiberg–Witten and Chern–Weil estimates force any near-counterexample in the LeBrun blow-up family into the critical regime \(k/A\to1/3\) and produce explicit topology-normalized scalar, Weyl-modulus, and tensor-eigenvalue deficits [Steps 3–8];
- Derdziński’s source-verified local theorem forbids the resulting calibrated spectrum on an open \(\operatorname{Ric}=-g\) Einstein germ [Steps 6–8];
- collapse, cusp, Taub–NUT, orbit-volume, and Kaluza–Klein analyses showed that local nilpotent symmetry and mixed curvature are not themselves contradictions; the missing bridge is access to controlled fixed-scale geometry carrying the normalized deficits [Steps 8–14];
- Noether and Chern–Weil supply the \(O(A)\) full-curvature budget needed for selected maximal-function good supports [Steps 10–14];
- fixed-scale smoothing is compatible with the nonzero Einstein background because Li’s smallness is dimensionless, but the Step 15 claim that a plateau and finite propagation localized the flow was false and was withdrawn [Steps 14–16];
- exponential-pullback averaging simplified the desired post-smoothing passage and may avoid a full collapse-rank classification [Steps 16–17];
- weighted cutoff analysis, Whitney scaling, and repeated normalization corrections identified the correct collapse-invariant quantities and rejected false local-volume, all-exponent, and transition-curvature claims [Steps 18–22];
- a graph persistence theorem was developed but then correctly restricted to an unavailable all-centers hypothesis; the active route uses separated selected good supports with stationary collars [Steps 23–24];
- buffered tensor calculations established the expected q=2, weighted q=3, and triangular defect structures at a schematic and independently cross-checked level, while global normalized defect can be recovered by an exact stationary-complement identity [Steps 24–26];
- fixed \(J_6\) defect energy, Yang’s source, and the three-factor weak Moser decomposition now give a coherent conditional mechanism for both support-wide weighted curvature and integrable weighted velocity [Steps 26–27];
- the remaining analytic burden is to prove the complete weak tensor hierarchy and normalized first-exit continuation theorem, not merely short-time existence or plateau regularity [Steps 26–27];
- after that, terminal Seiberg–Witten recalibration and a plateau-access/noncollapse or exponential-pullback argument are still needed before the Derdziński contradiction becomes a complete conditional gap theorem [Step 27].

The research has therefore converted a broad counterexample search into a sharply specified sequence of analytic and geometric obligations. Several earlier “completion” claims were corrected rather than retained: the Lohkamp shortcut, naive ALE scaling exclusion, Kähler blow-up route, orbit-volume exclusion, Hessian positivity, all-centers Li localization, finite-propagation cutoff argument, Whitney-volume-normal energy, all-exponent critical absorption, transition curvature closeness, plateau-only metric stability, and direct scalar invocation of Yang B.1 are all superseded by the current formulation [Steps 1–27].

Even full completion of the present cutoff-flow and plateau-access program would exclude only the critical LeBrun/Ishida–LeBrun negative counterexample laboratory. It would not establish the full four-dimensional negative branch, the positive branch, dimensions \(n\ge5\), the original interval proposition, or Lean formalization [Steps 1–27].

# Results, Observations, and Their Meaning

## Logical formulation and classical baselines

- For each fixed dimension \(n\), the interval proposition \(Q_n\) is equivalent to proving at least one normalized sign branch \(P_n^+\) or \(P_n^-\). After choosing a same-sign subinterval and rescaling, these ask for a dimension-only \(\varepsilon_n>0\) such that
  \[
  \|g^{-1}\operatorname{Ric}_g-\sigma I\|_{\infty,\mathrm{op}}<\varepsilon_n,
  \qquad \sigma\in\{+1,-1\},
  \]
  forces the underlying smooth manifold to admit some Einstein metric. Either sign proves \(Q_n\); refuting \(Q_n\) requires defeating both signs in the same dimension. [Steps 1–3]

- Dimension three is a classical baseline rather than an original result. Since \(W=0\), if the Ricci eigenvalues lie within \(\delta<1/3\) of \(\sigma\), then
  \[
  K_{ij}=\frac{r_i+r_j-r_k}{2}
  \]
  has sign \(\sigma\). Positive sectional curvature leads through Hamilton to a spherical Einstein metric; the negative case proceeds through negatively curved topology and geometrization to a hyperbolic metric. [Steps 2–3]

- Min–Oo’s primary hypothesis was corrected from an OCR-induced average-scalar expression to a scale-invariant bounded-geometry condition of the form
  \[
  d(0)^2\max |K(0)|<\Lambda^2.
  \]
  For \(n>3\), his theorem gives a negative Einstein metric from a compact negative almost-Einstein metric under this control. The proof uses normalized Ricci flow, \(L^2\) decay of trace-free Ricci, Sobolev/Moser estimates, parabolic regularity, and convergence. Thus a negative countersequence can evade the theorem through diameter divergence, full-curvature concentration, or another loss of controlled geometry; Weyl blow-up alone is not required. [Steps 1–2]

- Lohkamp’s retrieved work proves extensive one-sided negative-Ricci flexibility, including \(\operatorname{Ric}<0\) on every closed \(n\ge3\) manifold and localized curvature-decreasing deformations. None of the inspected sources constructs arbitrary two-sided normalized pinching
  \[
  \|g^{-1}\operatorname{Ric}_g+I\|_{\infty,\mathrm{op}}\to0.
  \]
  Local second-jet openness and one-sided \(h\)-principles therefore do not globalize to the needed counterexamples. [Steps 1–2]

- The exact original wording of Yau’s Problem 26, Anderson 1989 Corollary B(4), and Ye 1993 was not recovered. The Seminar on Differential Geometry metadata places the Problem Section at printed page 669 but does not expose Problem 26. Anderson and Ye remained at metadata or partial-access level and cannot support unverified hypotheses. [Step 1]

## Four-dimensional topological constraints

- For a closed oriented four-manifold,
  \[
  \delta_\sigma(g)=\|g^{-1}\operatorname{Ric}_g-\sigma I\|_{\infty,\mathrm{op}}
  <\frac1{1+\sqrt3}
  \]
  implies
  \[
  2\chi>3|\tau|.
  \]
  Hence Hitchin–Thorpe equality or violation uniformly obstructs arbitrarily tight pinching of either sign. This is only necessary; strict Hitchin–Thorpe does not imply Einstein existence. [Step 1]

- The corrected connected-sum arithmetic is
  \[
  \chi(\#_m\mathbb{CP}^2)=m+2,\qquad
  \tau(\#_m\mathbb{CP}^2)=m,\qquad
  2\chi-3\tau=4-m.
  \]
  Thus \(m=4\) is equality, \(m\ge5\) violates Hitchin–Thorpe, and \(m=3\) is not excluded. The earlier \(2-m\) formula was repaired. Tight pinching itself forces strict Hitchin–Thorpe, so violators cannot serve as tightly pinched counterexamples. [Steps 3–4, 8–9]

## LeBrun blow-ups and the mixed Seiberg–Witten gap

- For
  \[
  M=X\#k\overline{\mathbb{CP}}^{\,2},\qquad A=c_1^2(X),
  \]
  LeBrun’s original scalar argument obstructs Einstein metrics for \(k\ge2A/3\). The mixed Seiberg–Witten estimate strengthens the strict obstruction range to \(k>A/3\), under the stated monopole-class and orientation assumptions. These manifolds are a reservoir of no-Einstein topologies, but no tightly negative-Ricci-pinched metrics on them have been constructed. [Steps 1–4]

- The verified source-level estimate is
  \[
  \frac1{4\pi^2}\int_M
  \left(\frac{s^2}{24}+2|W^+|^2\right)d\mu
  \ge \frac23(a^+)^2.
  \]
  Its proof uses the Seiberg–Witten spinor Weitzenböck formula, a self-dual-form Weitzenböck formula, conformal minimization involving \(s+3w\), and norm/Cauchy–Schwarz inequalities. It is not a Weyl-only estimate and does not assume that \(F_A^+\) is simply harmonic. Equality yields special almost-Kähler geometry; on blow-ups exact equality is ruled out by Taubes’ positive-area argument for exceptional spheres. [Steps 3–4]

- Choosing signs among monopole classes gives \((a^+)^2\ge A\). Define
  \[
  I=\frac1{4\pi^2}\int\left(\frac{s^2}{24}+2|W^+|^2\right),\quad
  J=\frac1{4\pi^2}\int\frac{|\mathring{\operatorname{Ric}}|^2}{2},\quad
  q=k-\frac A3.
  \]
  Chern–Gauss–Bonnet gives \(I-J=A-k\). Combining this identity with pointwise normalized Ricci pinching yields
  \[
  \frac{\delta}{1-\delta}
  \ge
  \sqrt{\frac{k/A-1/3}{2}}
  \qquad(k/A>1/3).
  \]
  Therefore a uniform gap is established whenever \(k/A\) remains uniformly above \(1/3\); only the boundary regime \(k/A\downarrow1/3\) can support a hypothetical \(\delta\to0\) sequence. [Steps 2–3]

- Averaging all \(2^k\) sign choices gives
  \[
  2^{-k}\sum_\varepsilon(a_\varepsilon^+)^2
  =A+\sum_j(E_j^+)^2,
  \]
  hence
  \[
  J\ge q+\frac23\sum_j(E_j^+)^2.
  \]
  Any boundary sequence with \(\delta\to0\) and \(q/A\to0\) must satisfy
  \[
  \frac1A\sum_j(E_j^+)^2\to0.
  \]
  This is a metric consequence of the monopole estimates, not an abstract intersection-form theorem. [Steps 3–4]

- The direct volume estimate
  \[
  4\pi^2(A-k)\ge
  \left[\frac23(1-\delta)^2-2\delta^2\right]\operatorname{Vol}(g)
  \]
  implies \(\operatorname{Vol}(g)/A=O(1)\) near the boundary. Moreover,
  \[
  q\le J=O(\delta^2A),\qquad
  \frac{k}{A}=\frac13+O(\delta^2).
  \]
  For
  \[
  D_a=I-\frac23(a^+)^2,
  \]
  one has
  \[
  D_a=J-q-\frac23\bigl((a^+)^2-A\bigr),\qquad
  0\le D_a\le J-q,
  \]
  so \(D_a/A=O(\delta^2)\). This is normalized global control; it does not imply \(D_a\to0\) absolutely or local saturation on every bounded-volume region. [Steps 4–6]

## Calibrated Weyl remainder and forbidden local germ

- The final Cauchy–Schwarz remainder is
  \[
  \int_M\bigl(s+8\sqrt6\,|W^+|\bigr)^2\,d\mu
  \le864\pi^2D_a.
  \]
  Thus the boundary regime forces, in \(A\)-normalized mean,
  \[
  s\to-4,\qquad |W^+|\to\frac1{2\sqrt6}.
  \]
  Once the eigenvalue slack also vanishes, the calibrated spectrum is
  \[
  \operatorname{spec}(W^+)
  =\left(\frac1{12},\frac1{12},-\frac16\right),
  \qquad |W^+|^2=\frac1{24}.
  \]
  These eigenvalues and the norm are one quarter, not one half, of those of a four-dimensional Kähler–Einstein metric with \(\operatorname{Ric}=-g\), whose \(W^+\) spectrum is \((1/3,1/3,-2/3)\) and norm squared \(2/3\). [Steps 5–8]

- A macroscopic \(\operatorname{Ric}=-g\) Kähler–Einstein exterior is incompatible with the remainder. At such a point,
  \[
  \bigl(s+8\sqrt6|W^+|\bigr)^2=144.
  \]
  Hence Kähler–Einstein geometry cannot occupy volume comparable to \(A\) in a boundary sequence. This does not exclude small collars, non-Kähler Einstein exteriors, or corrected ALE gluing. [Step 5]

- Norm control alone does not fix eigenspaces. For eigenvalues
  \[
  \alpha\ge\beta\ge\gamma=w,\qquad \alpha+\beta+\gamma=0,
  \]
  one has
  \[
  |W^+|^2-\frac32w^2=\frac12(\alpha-\beta)^2.
  \]
  The full two-eigenvalue calibration therefore needs control of
  \[
  \xi=w+\sqrt{\frac23}|W^+|.
  \]
  Scalar spinor-norm estimates do not control the spinor direction, its connection, or the associated self-dual form. [Steps 6–7]

- Writing
  \[
  u=|W^+|,\quad
  f=\frac23s-2\sqrt{\frac23}u,\quad
  a_*=\frac23s+2w,
  \]
  the nonnegative substitution gap is
  \[
  G=f^2-(a_*{}_-)^2.
  \]
  The algebraic identity
  \[
  \frac{s^2}{24}+2u^2
  =\frac{f^2}{12}
   +\frac{(s+8\sqrt6\,u)^2}{216}
  \]
  was symbolically checked, and LeBrun’s inequalities imply
  \[
  \int_M G\le48\pi^2D_a.
  \]
  At \(s=-4\), \(u=1/(2\sqrt6)\), vanishing \(G\) forces \(\xi=0\), hence the calibrated spectrum. This explicit tensor deficit is the verified mechanism for passing the spectrum to local limits. Proposed substitutes based on local harmonic-form mass or unique continuation were rejected because a nonzero global harmonic form can converge to zero on every selected chart, and one eigenform does not determine all Weyl eigenvalues. [Steps 7–8, 16]

- In the fully saturated regime,
  \[
  \frac{\operatorname{Vol}(g)}{\pi^2A}\to\frac{32}{9},
  \qquad
  \frac1{\pi^2A}\int|W^+|^2\to\frac4{27}.
  \]
  These are normalized global integral limits, not pointwise convergence statements. [Steps 5–8]

- Derdziński’s original 1983 Proposition 5 was recovered directly. On \(\{W^+\ne0\}\), an oriented four-metric with \(\delta W^+=0\) and at most two \(W^+\) eigenvalues is locally conformal to a Kähler metric by
  \[
  (24|W^+|^2)^{1/3}g,
  \]
  with essential uniqueness. [Step 8]

- Consequently, a smooth Einstein limit satisfying
  \[
  \operatorname{Ric}=-g,\qquad
  |W^+|^2=\frac1{24},\qquad
  \operatorname{spec}(W^+)=\left(\frac1{12},\frac1{12},-\frac16\right)
  \]
  is impossible: the conformal factor is constant, so the metric is locally Kähler, while a Kähler Einstein four-metric with \(s=-4\) must satisfy \(|W^+|^2=s^2/24=2/3\). This is a local forbidden-germ theorem, conditional only on obtaining a smooth Einstein limit carrying the calibrated profile. [Steps 7–8]

- An independent projector/Bochner calculation gives the same contradiction. Harmonic \(W^+\) with the calibrated constant two-eigenvalue spectrum forces the simple self-dual eigenform to be parallel and \(\nabla W^+=0\). The corrected Einstein Weyl Bochner identity, with coefficients \(s/2\) and \(-6\), instead requires
  \[
  |\nabla W^+|^2=\frac1{16}.
  \]
  Earlier coefficients \(s/3,-4\) and the value \(1/24\) were corrected. [Steps 7–8]

## Compactness, averaging, and accessibility

- On a supplied controlled harmonic chart, only finite-\(p\) strong \(W^{2,p}\) convergence is needed. In harmonic coordinates,
  \[
  g^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b g
  =-2\operatorname{Ric}(g)+Q(g^{-1},\partial g).
  \]
  Controlled harmonic radius, \(C^{1,\alpha}\) convergence, and uniform \(\operatorname{Ric}(g_i)+g_i\to0\) give strong interior \(W^{2,p}\) convergence; the weak Einstein limit bootstraps smoothly. Finite-\(p\) curvature convergence passes scalar, norm, and eigenvalue-gap deficits because curvature-operator eigenvalues depend Lipschitz-continuously on matrix entries. Unsupported \(C^{2,\alpha}\) convergence of the approximating metrics was not used. [Steps 7–8, 10–11]

- Cheeger–Naber gives measure estimates for small harmonic radius under bounded Ricci, but not harmonic radius at every point. Its four-dimensional theorem includes bounded Ricci, noncollapse, and diameter hypotheses. Naber–Zhang’s local-universal-cover harmonic-radius theorem additionally requires residual dimension \(\le3\), maximal fibered nilpotency rank, a model noncollapsing scale, and local completeness; its stronger curvature estimate assumes Einstein or \(\nabla\operatorname{Ric}\) control. [Steps 7, 9–11]

- For a nonnegative deficit \(F_i\), volume-random selection and doubling yield
  \[
  \mathbb E\!\left[\fint_{B_R(p)}F_i\right]
  \le C(R)\fint_{M_i}F_i.
  \]
  Applied to the LeBrun boundary sequence, this proves
  \[
  \frac{\operatorname{Vol}\{p:\operatorname{Vol}(B_1(p))\ge v\}}
       {\operatorname{Vol}(M_i)}\to0
  \]
  for each fixed \(v>0\); otherwise a noncollapsed chart with vanishing deficits would produce the forbidden germ. The conclusion is collapse in volume proportion, not uniform collapse; a bounded-volume noncollapsed island may remain negligible relative to \(A\). [Steps 7–8]

- A point was termed accessible when a fixed buffered local domain has a genuine normal cover with fixed-radius noncollapse and a controlled harmonic chart. Compactness plus the forbidden germ gives a positive local defect gap for every fixed control package, so the volume proportion of accessible points must vanish in a boundary sequence. This separates the local analytic contradiction from any particular collapse theorem. [Steps 10–11]

- For a genuine normal cover
  \[
  \pi:(\widehat U,\hat g)\to(U,g)
  \]
  with \(\operatorname{Ric}_{\hat g}\ge-(n-1)K\hat g\) and a \(3r\) buffer,
  \[
  \fint_{B_r(\hat p)}\pi^*\phi
  \le
  \frac{V_K(3r)}{V_K(r)}
  \fint_{B_r(p)}\phi
  \]
  for every nonnegative measurable \(\phi\). The proof uses a measurable section, deck-transformation multiplicity, disjoint translates inside \(B_{3r}(\hat p)\), and Bishop–Gromov comparison; sheet number cancels. It does not automatically apply to pseudogroups, truncated covers without buffer, or unwrapping available only at shrinking scales. [Steps 9–10]

- Once bounded-sectional-curvature buffers exist, exponential-pullback averaging can avoid cover topology. Pulling back by \(\exp_p\), Rauch estimates control Jacobians and Liouville invariance supports averaging deficit densities on tangent-space balls. This is a plausible post-smoothing selection mechanism, but is conditional on first producing bounded-curvature buffered plateaux of positive volume. [Steps 16–18]

- Lott’s adapted abelian equation

  \Delta_B\sqrt{\det G}
  =\left(\frac{|F|^2}{4}-\lambda N\right)\sqrt{\det G}
  \]
  was verified from the primary source. The relevant proposition also assumes parabolicity, \(\lambda\le0\), bounded orbit volume, and determinant-line holonomy. Thus it does not obstruct local interval-base abelian collapse. The hyperbolic torus cusp

  dt^2+e^{2t/\sqrt3}g_{T^3},\qquad \operatorname{Ric}=-g,

  is an immediate calibration. [Step 10]

- For the Bianchi II/Nil\(^3\) ansatz,
  \[
  \mu=\frac{a_3^2}{2a_1^2a_2^2},\qquad v=a_1a_2a_3,
  \]
  the corrected Einstein equation is
  \[
  \frac{v''}{v}=3-\mu.
  \]
  The prior \(3+\mu\) formula was retracted. It is verified by the complex-hyperbolic cusp
  \[
  a_1=a_2=e^{s/\sqrt6},\qquad
  a_3=\sqrt{\frac23}e^{2s/\sqrt6},
  \]
  for which \(\mu=1/3\) and \(v''/v=8/3\). Exact circle-base Nil collapse still requires an additional periodic identity, for example
  \[
  (vf_3)'=(1+\mu)v>0;
  \]
  it does not follow from \(v''/v=3-\mu\) alone. [Steps 9–10]

- Corrected four-dimensional curvature bookkeeping is
  \[
  12\pi^2\tau(M)=\int(|W^+|^2-|W^-|^2),
  \]
  and, in the adopted curvature-operator convention,
  \[
  \int|\mathcal R|^2
  =8\pi^2\chi(M)+\int|\mathring{\operatorname{Ric}}|^2
  =8\pi^2\bigl(\chi(X)+k+J\bigr).
  \]
  The former erroneous added \(32\pi^2k\) term omitted the contribution from \(X\). [Steps 10–11]

- Noether gives \(A\ge2p_g-4\), while
  \[
  \chi_{\mathrm{hol}}\le p_g+1,\qquad
  \chi_{\mathrm{top}}=12\chi_{\mathrm{hol}}-A,
  \]
  hence \(\chi_{\mathrm{top}}(X)\le5A+36\). For the standard Ishida–LeBrun input with \(b_+(N)=0\), connected-sum arithmetic gives the usable bound

  \]
  This yields uniformly bounded global mean curvature-operator energy in the boundary family, but not harmonic radius, pointwise curvature, cover noncollapse, or regular neighborhoods. Bogomolov–Miyaoka–Yau has the wrong direction for the desired upper bound. [Steps 11, 18]

- In the calibrated regime,
  \[
  P=2|W^+|^2+\frac{s^2}{24}
    -\frac{|\mathring{\operatorname{Ric}}|^2}{2}
  \]
  satisfies
  \[
  \fint_M|P-\tfrac34|\to0.
  \]
  Regions of volume \(o(A)\) carry only \(o(A)\) physical Pontryagin mass; order-\(A\) characteristic mass is diffuse through the calibrated bulk rather than concentrated in small NUT cores. A basic \(\Lambda^2_+\) connection pulled back from a base of dimension at most three has vanishing Pontryagin four-form, but non-basic mixed curvature, scaled holonomy, O’Neill tensors, fiber-length gradients, frame twist, and transition flux can distribute charge in collapsed regions. Consequently, NUT-count or fixed-defect-per-NUT arguments were rejected. [Steps 11–12]

- Exact Taub–NUT–AdS calculations verify \(\operatorname{Ric}=-g\), \(s=-4\), and the curvature-operator trace convention. In the source orientation,
  \[
  \operatorname{Spec}(W^-)=(a,a,-2a),\qquad
  a=\frac{2\nu(4\nu^2-3)}{3(r+\nu)^3},
  \]
  with
  \[
  |W|^2
  =\frac{32\nu^2(4\nu^2-3)^2}{3(r+\nu)^6}.
  \]
  A large fixed-radius ball containing the NUT has mean Weyl energy asymptotic to \(3/(\nu R^3)\), so it violates uniform mean-energy control as \(\nu\to0\), and its cover cannot unwrap the Hopf fiber because that fiber contracts through the NUT. On a fixed annulus avoiding the core, a Hopf-trivializing cover does unwrap and converges to real hyperbolic four-space of sectional curvature \(-1/3\). Thus large-domain cover failure does not exclude smaller accessible domains. [Steps 11–12]

- In the opposite orientation, the shell where \(|W^+|^2=1/24\) occurs at

  \]
  but has the wrong sign pattern, recorded calibrated defect \(35/36\), and no fixed physical-scale calibrated region. Derdziński forbids an open calibrated Einstein region, not an isolated radius satisfying one scalar equality. [Step 12]

- Rank-one Kaluza–Klein normalization,
  \[
  g=g_B+\ell^2(d\psi+A)^2,\qquad
  z=\ell(p)\psi,\quad v=\ell/\ell(p),\quad B=\ell(p)A,

  gives

  on the unwrapped domain. The absolute short-fiber period disappears from the local coefficients; accessibility depends on normalized base geometry, \(v\), gauge-fixed \(B\), derivatives, a buffered fibration domain, and survival of the fiber in local \(\pi_1\). [Steps 12–13]

- Verified rank-one equations include
  \[
  \operatorname{div}(v^3F)=0
  \quad\text{equivalently}\quad
  \delta(v^2C)=0,
  \]
  and
  \[
  \operatorname{tr}H+|u|^2=1+\frac{|C|^2}{2}.
  \]
  The chiral factorization

  a_\pm=u\mp z/2,\qquad
  W^\pm=-[\operatorname{sym}\nabla a_\pm+a_\pm\otimes a_\pm]_0,
  \qquad da_+=a_+\wedge a_-

  shows that calibration controls only one trace-free symmetric chiral derivative; antisymmetric and trace modes retain freedom. [Step 13]

- The exact identity

  H=\frac13I+\frac14(|z|^2I-z\otimes z)
  -\frac12(W^++W^-)

  shows that calibrated \(W^+\) does not force \(H\ge0\). If

  then

## Initial smoothing evidence and its limitations

- Ye Li’s four-dimensional theorem assumes the dimensionless condition
  \[
  r^4\fint_{B_r(x)}|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{Li}},
  \]
  not small curvature at unit scale. On a maximal-function good support with mean curvature energy \(K_0\), one can choose a sufficiently small but fixed physical radius \(r_*\) so that \(K_0r_*^4\ll1\). The normalized \(\operatorname{Ric}\approx-g\) scale therefore remains nonzero. [Steps 14–15]

- In four dimensions, collapse cancels from the critical Sobolev product:
  \[
  A_U\|\operatorname{Rm}\|_{L^2(U)}
  \lesssim\sqrt{K_0}\,r^2,
  \]
  when
  \[
  A_U\sim\frac{r^2}{\operatorname{Vol}(U)^{1/2}},\qquad
  \int_U|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\lesssim K_0\operatorname{Vol}(U).
  \]
  In dimension \(n\), the formal analogue is
  \[
  A_U\|\operatorname{Rm}\|_{L^{n/2}}
  \lesssim
  r^2\left(\fint_U|\operatorname{Rm}|^{n/2}\right)^{2/n}.
  \]
  This critical cancellation is reusable, but the topology-driven \(L^{n/2}\) input is currently specific to the four-dimensional laboratory. [Steps 15, 17–18]

- Comparable-scale Bishop–Gromov transfer is valid, with a coarse factor near \(1785\) for the radii used in the support architecture. Earlier macro-to-micro volume-ratio transfer was invalid. Supports \(B_{5r_*}\) require initial maximal-function control through at least \(B_{6r_*}\). [Steps 15, 17–18]

- Li’s theorem is complete/all-centers. Ricci flow has no finite propagation, so a plateau cannot shield an inner region from uncontrolled transition geometry. The Step 15 localized-Li completion and Step 17 plateau-bootstrap claims were withdrawn because their evolving supremum required neighboring balls outside the controlled domain. Enlarging the plateau fixed containment but not the closed-supremum issue. [Steps 15–18]

## Development of the weighted cutoff-flow mechanism

- The localized flow is
  \[
  \partial_tg=-2aE,\qquad
  a=\chi^2,\qquad
  E=\operatorname{Ric}+g.
  \]
  Exact \(\operatorname{Ric}=-g\) metrics are stationary, including across the transition. Three quantities must remain distinct:
  1. \(a\,\operatorname{Rm}\), for weighted curvature and smoothing;
  2. \(aE\), for metric velocity;
  3. unweighted \(Q(t)=\int|E|^2\), for terminal topological recalibration.
  
  A pointwise bound on \(aE\) does not directly control \(Q\) where \(a\to0\). [Steps 16–18]

- For the scalar weighted curvature variable \(f=a|\operatorname{Rm}|\), the principal algebra is favorable:
  \[
  \partial_tf
  \lesssim a\Delta f-2\langle\nabla a,\nabla f\rangle
  +\left(\frac{2|\nabla a|^2}{a}-\Delta a\right)f
  +Cf^2+aT.
  \]
  The nonlinear reaction is \(Cf^2\), not \(Cf^2/a\), and
  \[
  \frac{|\nabla a|^2}{a}=4|\nabla\chi|^2.
  \]
  At the integrated scalar level, the explicit \(\Delta a\) term cancels by parts. The tensor equation still contains \(\nabla^2a*E*\operatorname{Rm}\), \(\nabla a*\nabla E*\operatorname{Rm}\), and algebraic terms, so scalar evidence alone did not establish continuation. [Step 18]

### Whitney reduction and corrections

- On a Whitney ball centered where \(\chi=\chi_0>0\), choose
  \[
  \ell=cr\chi_0.
  \]
  With \(c=0.1\) and the recorded gradient bound, \(a/a_0\) lies in approximately \([0.640,1.440]\); scaled drift and potential remain bounded, and the ratio of diffusion length to Whitney radius is independent of \(\chi_0\). Thus cutoff degeneracy becomes a uniformly parabolic local problem after Whitney scaling. [Steps 18–19]

- From a support energy bound and initial Bishop–Gromov comparison,
  \[
  \ell^4\fint_{B_\ell(y)}|\operatorname{Rm}|^2
  \le C K_0r^4
  \]
  uniformly as \(\chi_0\to0\). The Sobolev absorption product also satisfies
  \[
  A_\ell^2\|\operatorname{Rm}\|_2
  \lesssim C\sqrt{K_0}\,r^2,
  \]
  independently of \(\chi_0\) and collapsed volume. Physical time \(\theta r^2\) corresponds to the same normalized Whitney diffusion time at every cutoff level. These are genuine cancellation mechanisms. [Step 19]

- Several Step 19 bookkeeping corrections were essential: \(a-a_0=O(ca_0)\), not \(O(c^2a_0)\); localization costs scale like \(\exp(C\theta/c^2)\); support energy is local per component; the relevant Sobolev coefficient is squared; overlap controls unnormalized integrals only; and curvature and defect energies cannot initially be treated as unrelated scalar fields. [Step 19]

- Since
  \[
  E=\operatorname{Ric}+g,\qquad \nabla E=\operatorname{contr}(\nabla\operatorname{Rm}),
  \]
  the \(\nabla E\) terms arising after integrating \(\nabla^2a\) by parts can be absorbed into the full tensor curvature dissipation. Also \(|E|\lesssim(1+|\operatorname{Rm}|^2)^{1/2}\). This changed the high-power curvature layer from an abstract two-field iteration into a curvature-only tensor inequality plus a separate triangular defect estimate. [Step 20]

- Direct all-exponent critical absorption was rejected because the threshold deteriorates with the power \(q\). The viable plan became a fixed-exponent critical upgrade, followed by a positive-time subcritical iteration. An additive estimate of the form \(Q'\lesssim \varepsilon X+\cdots\) was also rejected: if \(\int X=O(A)\), it leaves \(O(\varepsilon A)\), not \(o(A)\). Preservation of \(Q/A\to0\) requires a homogeneous triangular defect equation in which curvature multiplies \(|E|^2\). [Step 20]

- The proposed fixed-exponent chain \(q=2\to\) spacetime \(L^3\to q=3\to\) time-uniform spatial \(L^3\) is structurally appropriate in dimension four. Spacetime \(L^3\) alone is parabolically critical; the q=3 time-cutoff step is needed before a final mean-value argument. [Step 21]

- A rescaled Stampacchia argument in Step 21 had a decisive scaling error:
  \[
  \tilde g=\ell^{-2}g
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  |\operatorname{Rm}(\tilde g)|=\ell^2|\operatorname{Rm}(g)|.
  \]
  Its raw output was only \(\ell^2F\le C\), equivalently \(a|\operatorname{Rm}|\lesssim r^{-2}\), not the sharper claimed estimate. That weaker terminal estimate would still be scientifically adequate on fixed-radius plateaux, but could not be used as the asserted stability estimate. [Step 21]

- A second normalization error was repaired in Step 22. From a component energy budget
  \[
  \int_\Omega F^2\le M\operatorname{Vol}(\Omega),
  \]
  one cannot conclude a Whitney-volume-normal bound on every \(B_\ell\). A nonconcentric \(9r\)-buffer comparison allows the local mean to grow like \((r/\ell)^4\sim\chi_0^{-4}\). What remains uniformly controlled is
  \[
  \ell^4\fint_{B_\ell}F^2
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  A_\ell^2\|F\|_2.
  \]
  This forced all subsequent estimates to carry relative Sobolev coefficients and current support energies explicitly rather than interchange component budgets, local means, and rescaled integrals. [Step 22]

### Conditional graph argument and why it was not applicable

- A cooperative graph formulation used
  \[
  S_\alpha=A_\alpha^4H_{2,\alpha}.
  \]
  For a vector inequality
  \[
  S'+cZ\le br^{-2}BS+\varepsilon BZ,
  \]
  with a nonnegative bounded-row-sum matrix \(B\), the positive resolvent
  \[
  P=(I-\rho B)^{-1},\qquad \varepsilon/c<\rho<1/\|B\|_{\mathrm{row}},
  \]
  yields localized component-count-independent control because
  \[
  PB=(P-I)/\rho.
  \]
  This is a valid conditional graph lemma. [Steps 22–23]

- The Sobolev variable on one component has local dissipation:
  \[
  v=\eta_\alpha a^{1/2}F,
  \]
  and
  \[
  |\nabla v|^2
  \lesssim \eta_\alpha^2a|\nabla F|^2
  +\eta_\alpha^2\frac{|\nabla a|^2}{a}F^2
  +a|\nabla\eta_\alpha|^2F^2.
  \]
  Thus no neighbor dissipation is intrinsically required. A maximal \(r\)-net would also give \(\sum\eta_\beta^2\ge1\), repairing a prior uncovered annulus. [Step 23]

- That maximal-net repair is unusable for the actual sequence: it introduces centers outside the maximal-function good set, where no small initial critical product is available. The graph theorem therefore remains conditional on all-center smallness and cannot replace Li’s all-centers hypothesis in the selected-good-support setting. [Step 24]

### Buffered selected supports

- The current localization separates the physical cutoff \(\chi\) from an auxiliary energy cutoff \(\eta\):
  \[
  \operatorname{supp}\chi\Subset\{\eta=1\},\qquad
  \operatorname{supp}\nabla\eta\subset\{\chi=0\}.
  \]
  Consequently
  \[
  a|\nabla\eta|^2=0,\qquad
  \nabla a\cdot\nabla\eta=0.
  \]
  The collar is exactly stationary because \(a=0\) there; this is a support identity, not finite propagation. The entire active transition remains inside the controlled energy domain. [Step 24]

- On a selected maximal-function good support \(\Omega\),
  \[
  \beta_0
  =A_\Omega^2\|F(0)\|_{L^2(\operatorname{supp}\chi)}
  \lesssim r^2\sqrt{1+K_0},
  \qquad F=(1+|\operatorname{Rm}|^2)^{1/2},
  \]
  with collapsed volume cancelling. The radius must be chosen after the support ratios and tensor constants. An illustrative script found \(r=0.003\) too large for its sample constants and \(r=1.71322\times10^{-3}\) sufficient to give \(\beta=0.025\); these values are scaling checks, not PDE thresholds. [Step 24]

- Static maximal-function selection, separated packing, and bounded-degree coloring retain a sequence-independent positive plateau fraction. The crude sample bound was only about \(6.74\times10^{-10}\) when the good set occupied half the manifold, but positivity independent of collapse and \(A\) is what the downstream averaging argument would need. [Step 24]

## Tensor energy inequalities and normalization correction

- The buffered-support tensor calculation was developed schematically in Step 25 and independently reproduced by the completed Codex worker in Step 26. For \(F=(1+|\operatorname{Rm}|^2)^{1/2}\), the local curvature target is
  \[
  H_2'+cD_2
  \le C\int \eta^2aF^3+Cr^{-2}H_2+C_0,
  \]
  where \(C_0=O(\operatorname{Vol}\Omega)\) comes from the constant part of \(F^2\). The derivation classifies:
  - principal Bochner diffusion and tensor dissipation;
  - \(\nabla a\cdot\nabla E\cdot\operatorname{Rm}\), absorbed using \(|\nabla a|^2/a=4|\nabla\chi|^2\);
  - \(\nabla^2a*E*\operatorname{Rm}\), integrated by parts;
  - algebraic curvature/defect coupling;
  - moving inverse metric, norm, and volume form.
  
  The stationary-collar arrangement eliminates mixed \(\nabla a\)-\(\nabla\eta\) terms. [Steps 24–26]

- The tensor identity is
  \[
  \nabla^2a=2\,d\chi\otimes d\chi+2\chi\nabla^2\chi.
  \]
  It cannot be replaced by a scalar \(\Delta a\) pointwise. The inequalities are integrated tensor estimates; no pointwise scalar Kato equation with only \(\chi\Delta\chi\) has been established. [Steps 25, 27]

- A normalization correction was verified by the pure conformal test \(\partial_tg=-2g\). Although the \((0,4)\)-curvature tensor variation contains a \(-2aR_{ijkl}\) term, the four inverse-metric variations add \(+8a|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\) in the norm derivative. For \(g(t)=e^{-2t}g_0\),
  \[
  |\operatorname{Rm}|^2=e^{4t}|\operatorname{Rm}_0|^2,\qquad
  d\mu=e^{-4t}d\mu_0,
  \]
  so \(\int|\operatorname{Rm}|^2d\mu\) is constant in four dimensions. There is no free coercive damping of curvature from the normalization. For \(F^2=1+|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\), the residual conformal term is a bounded volume source. [Step 25]

- The q=3 weighted curvature inequality has the form
  \[
  Y'+cD_3
  \le Cr^{-2}Y+C\int\eta^2a^2F^4.
  \]
  The correct Sobolev variable is
  \[
  u=aF^{3/2},
  \]
  not \(\chi F^{3/2}\). It gives
  \[
  \int a^2F^4
  \le\|F\|_2\|aF^{3/2}\|_4^2
  \le C\beta_a(D_3+r^{-2}Y).
  \]
  The q=2 estimate controls the weighted spacetime moment \(\int\!\!\int aF^3\); it must not be identified with \(a^{3/2}F^3\) from a different parabolic-Sobolev expression. [Steps 24–26]

- The defect equation for \(E=\operatorname{Ric}+g\) is homogeneous in \(E\) and \(\nabla E\): when \(E=0\), the velocity vanishes, so no curvature-only or cutoff-Hessian source may remain after Ricci and normalization terms are combined. The local target is
  \[
  Q'+cX
  \le Cr^{-2}Q+C\int\eta^2aF|E|^2.
  \]
  Its potential is absorbed using \(\chi E\), preserving multiplicative rather than additive control. The exact schematic derivation was independently reproduced by the Codex report, but it still depends on current metric/Sobolev/cutoff control. [Steps 24–26]

- If disjoint selected supports satisfy \(Q_j(t)\le C Q_j(0)\), the global defect obeys an exact stationary-complement identity:
  \[
  Q_{\mathrm{global}}(t)-Q_{\mathrm{global}}(0)
  =\sum_j\bigl(Q_j(t)-Q_j(0)\bigr).
  \]
  Since the auxiliary supports are disjoint and \(0\le\eta_j\le1\),
  \[
  \sum_jQ_j(0)\le Q_{\mathrm{global}}(0),
  \]
  hence
  \[
  Q_{\mathrm{global}}(t)\le\max\{1,C\}Q_{\mathrm{global}}(0).
  \]
  Initial pinching gives \(Q_{\mathrm{global}}(0)\le4\delta^2\operatorname{Vol}(g_0)\), so the established volume bound would imply \(Q_{\mathrm{global}}(t)/A\to0\). This conditional global passage requires no defect selection on the frozen bad-curvature complement. [Step 25]

## Weighted defect, metric velocity, and unified weak Moser mechanism

- Plateau regularity alone does not preserve the support-wide analytic environment. Metric comparison on the active support requires
  \[
  V(t)=\int_0^t\|aE(s)\|_{L^\infty(\operatorname{supp}\chi)}\,ds,
  \]
  because
  \[
  e^{-2V(t)}g_0\le g(t)\le e^{2V(t)}g_0.
  \]
  The small factor \(a\) does not automatically control transition displacement: \(E\) can grow as \(a\to0\). The former inference that transition curvature remains close to its initial value under small metric displacement was withdrawn; curvature involves second derivatives and was never initially pointwise controlled. [Steps 22, 25–26]

- For fixed \(p>2\), introduce
  \[
  J_p=\int\eta^2a^{p-2}|E|^p.
  \]
  Its dissipation has weight
  \[
  Z_p=\int\eta^2a^{p-1}|E|^{p-2}|\nabla E|^2,
  \]
  and the curvature potential factors through
  \[
  z_p=\eta a^{(p-1)/2}|E|^{p/2},\qquad
  \int\eta^2a^{p-1}F|E|^p=\int Fz_p^2.
  \]
  The transition remainder is regular:
  \[
  a^{p-3}|\nabla a|^2|E|^p
  =4|\nabla\chi|^2a^{p-2}|E|^p.
  \]
  Initial pinching gives \(J_p(0)\lesssim\delta^p\operatorname{Vol}(\Omega)\) without any higher-integrability assumption on full curvature. [Step 26]

- For \(p=6\),
  \[
  J_6=\int\eta^2\chi^8|E|^6,\qquad
  Z_6=\int\eta^2\chi^{10}|E|^4|\nabla E|^2.
  \]
  The variable \(\chi^5|E|^3\) must be justified by weak Kato or \((|E|^2+\varepsilon)^{3/2}\) regularization; \(|E|^3\) is not smooth at \(E=0\). [Step 26]

- Yang’s Appendix B has a striking weight match: with \(n=4\), \(p_0=q=6\), \(f=|E|\), and potential \(u=F\), its input weight is
  \[
  \chi^{2p_0-n}=\chi^8,
  \]
  and its potential quantity uses
  \[
  \left(\int\chi^{q-n}F^{q/2}\right)^{2/q}
  =\left(\int\chi^2F^3\right)^{1/3}.
  \]
  The dimensional scaling gives
  \[
  \|aE(t)\|_\infty
  \lesssim C\delta\left(\frac{r^2}{t}\right)^{1/3},
  \]
  and hence
  \[
  \int_0^{\theta r^2}\|aE(t)\|_\infty\,dt
  \lesssim \frac32C\delta r^2\theta^{2/3}.
  \]
  This is the desired integrable support-wide velocity scale. Direct invocation of Yang B.1 is not yet justified, however, because its scalar cutoff structure uses \(\chi\Delta\chi\), whereas the geometric defect equation contains anisotropic \(\nabla^2a\)-tensor contractions. [Steps 26–27]

- Step 27 replaced the attempted scalar reduction with a common weak tensor-power iteration. For either \(f=F\) or \(f=|E|\), define
  \[
  H_p(f)=\int a^{p-2}f^p,\qquad
  z_p=a^{(p-1)/2}f^{p/2},\qquad
  Y=\int aF^3.
  \]
  The exact algebraic factorization is
  \[
  a^{p-1}Ff^p
  =(aF^3)^{1/3}
   (a^{p-2}f^p)^{1/3}
   z_p^{4/3}.
  \]
  Hölder with exponents \(3,3,3\), followed by Sobolev and Young, turns the curvature reaction into a small multiple of \(\|\nabla z_p\|_2^2\) plus a coefficient of order
  \[
  S^2Y
  \]
  multiplying \(H_p\), where \(S\) is the squared relative Sobolev coefficient. This avoids a critical smallness threshold deteriorating at every exponent. Polynomial \(p\)-growth in the tensor energy constants is compatible with the Moser product. [Step 27]

- The same weak hierarchy has two different seeds:
  - Curvature: \(p_0=3\), \(H_3(F)=Y\). If
    \[
    S^2Y(s)\lesssim \beta^3/s
    \]
    on a positive-time slab, the iteration predicts
    \[
    \|aF(t)\|_\infty\lesssim C\beta/t.
    \]
  - Defect: \(p_0=6\), \(H_6(|E|)=J_6\lesssim\delta^6\operatorname{Vol}(\Omega)\), predicting
    \[
    \|aE(t)\|_\infty
    \lesssim C\delta(r^2/t)^{1/3}.
    \]
  
  In four dimensions the Sobolev/volume factors cancel exactly in both endpoints. The algebra, Hölder exponents, Moser-product convergence, and scaling cancellations were checked symbolically. These are conditional outputs of the weak tensor hierarchy, not yet an unconditional smoothing theorem. [Step 27]

## Local existence, DeTurck gauge, and continuation status

- Yang’s local Ricci-flow construction explicitly handles a fixed cutoff by using the transported hatted coefficient
  \[
  (\chi\circ\phi^{-1})^2
  \]
  in DeTurck gauge; pulling back by \(\phi\) restores the prescribed fixed spatial coefficient \(\chi^2\). For the normalized equation, the hatted system must place this coefficient in front of both \(\operatorname{Ric}(\hat g)\) and the lower-order \(\hat g\) term. This addresses the concern that gauge fixing might silently solve a different transported-cutoff equation. [Step 26]

- Smooth short-time existence for each smooth input is only a starting point; its lifespan may shrink with uncontrolled initial curvature peaks. The research requires a common time \(\theta r^2\) obtained from simultaneous weighted curvature, weighted velocity, energy, Sobolev, and metric-comparison control. Plateau Shi estimates do not create the first pointwise curvature bound from \(L^2\) data; they provide derivative control only after a curvature bound has been obtained. [Steps 25–26]

- The preferred continuation variable is the shifted curvature
  \[
  T=\operatorname{Rm}+G,\qquad
  G=\frac{g\owedge g}{2(n-1)},
  \]
  for which \(\operatorname{Ric}(T)=E\) and \(\nabla G=0\). With
  \[
  U=aT,
  \]
  the weighted equation has the same structural form as Wang’s local Ricci-flow extension system. The proposed normalized extension adapts Wang’s joint induction on
  \[
  \nabla^mU,\qquad \nabla^{m+1}\chi,
  \]
  rather than assuming evolving higher cutoff derivatives are uniformly bounded a priori. [Step 27]

- Earlier attempts to obtain extension by an \(\varepsilon\)-regularized strictly parabolic flow were withdrawn because uniform \(C^k\) estimates independent of \(\varepsilon\) were not established. Likewise, higher derivatives \(\nabla^i\chi\) depend on the evolving connection and cannot be treated as fixed numerical bounds beyond the first derivative. [Step 27]

- The assembled continuation theorem remains conditional on completing the exact general-\(p\) tensor weak hierarchy, establishing the positive-time cubic curvature potential, and verifying the shifted-curvature/Wang extension with the normalized lower-order term. Step 27’s notes and peer-session source establish a coherent proof architecture and checked algebra, not a fully audited autonomous theorem. [Step 27]

## Terminal recalibration and the remaining local-geometry gap

- If the local flow is completed and the global defect satisfies \(Q(T)/A\to0\), the mixed Seiberg–Witten inequality, Chern–Gauss–Bonnet, completion square, and explicit \(G\)-deficit should be reapplied directly to the terminal metric on the same closed smooth manifold. Terminal calibration must not be “transported” from \(g(0)\) merely by \(C^0\) metric comparison. The Seiberg–Witten and characteristic-number inequalities are topological and can be rerun for \(g(T)\). [Steps 15–18, 25, 27]

- Stationarity off the disjoint flow supports and support-wide metric comparison imply that \(\operatorname{Vol}(g(T))/A\) remains controlled. Conditional on \(Q(T)/A\to0\), the same calculations recover terminal normalized mean convergence to
  \[
  s=-4,\qquad |W^+|^2=\frac1{24},\qquad
  \operatorname{spec}(W^+)=\left(-\frac16,\frac1{12},\frac1{12}\right).
  \]
  Because selected plateaux occupy a fixed positive volume fraction, global nonnegative deficit averages can then be restricted/averaged over plateaux to select locations with small terminal defect. This terminal recalibration has been identified as the correct downstream chain but was not yet written as a fully checked theorem in Step 27. [Steps 25, 27]

- Bounded curvature on plateaux does not by itself give a smooth noncollapsed limit. The plateaux may collapse. Two unresolved routes were identified:
  1. combine the growth of Euler characteristic—recorded in the peer formulation as \(\chi(M)\ge1+8A/15\to\infty\)—with quantitative F-structure theory to show that not all bounded-curvature plateau geometry can collapse;
  2. use the earlier exponential-pullback averaging on bounded-curvature plateaux to obtain accessible tangent-space charts without a global noncollapse theorem.
  
  Either route must ensure that accessible/noncollapsed geometry intersects the positive-volume plateaux where terminal calibrated deficits vanish. No quantitative Euler-density localization or complete noncollapse/accessibility proof was obtained by Step 27. [Step 27]

- Therefore the four-dimensional negative LeBrun/Ishida–LeBrun route is still conditional at two levels: the weighted tensor continuation theorem and the terminal accessible-germ extraction. Even a successful completion would only exclude this critical counterexample laboratory; it would not prove \(P_4^-\) for arbitrary manifolds. [Steps 16–27]

## Positive branch, higher dimensions, and model gluing

- Positive pinching gives Myers diameter control, volume upper bounds, \(b_1=0\), finite fundamental group, and Gromov–Hausdorff precompactness after normalization. It gives no dimension-only volume lower bound or bound on \(|\pi_1|\); round lens-space quotients are exact positive Einstein metrics with arbitrarily small volume. Collapse therefore cannot simply be excluded. [Steps 5–7]

- Noncollapse plus two-sided Ricci bounds still does not automatically yield smooth convergence on the original manifold. Cheeger–Naber provides codimension-four/measure regularity, while Naber–Zhang and orbifold/ALE desingularization results have additional rank, model, bubble-tree, obstruction, and weighted-gluing hypotheses. None currently turns arbitrary positive near-Einstein metrics into Einstein metrics. [Steps 6–9]

- The peer positive-branch toric/Faber–Krahn/flux route remained specialized and conditional. A later toric audit gave a “BREAK” judgment: the proposed integral identities alone do not obstruct tight positive pinching on \(\#_k(S^2\times S^2)\). Kaluza–Klein examples also show that codimension-one positive collapse can be Einstein-compatible in dimensions \(n\ge5\). [Steps 14–27]

- Higher dimensions lack the four-dimensional \(W^+\), Seiberg–Witten, and Derdziński calibrated-germ mechanism. Although the critical Sobolev cancellation has an all-dimensional form, no all-dimensional topology-driven \(L^{n/2}\) input or forbidden local profile has been established. [Steps 18, 23–27]

- A bare Ricci-flat ALE core has normalized defect \(1\) relative to \(\operatorname{Ric}=-g\), independent of scale. This does not exclude corrected gluing: an \(O(t^2)\) relative correction to a core scaled by \(t^2\) can alter the original-scale Ricci endomorphism by order one. A nonzero first gluing obstruction appears to leave order-one normalized core defect; first-obstruction-zero but higher-obstruction-nonzero cases remain unresolved. [Steps 1, 3–4]

- Exact Taub–Bolt–AdS fillings demonstrate that exceptional-handle topology can occur locally with \(\operatorname{Ric}=-g\) for compatible interface data. A sweep over
  \[
  0<L^2\le\frac{2-\sqrt3}{4}\approx0.0669872981
  \]
  produced \(52{,}800\) samples. Under the sampled \(p=1\) convention, the two branches had \(b/a\) ranges approximately
  \[
  [0.007785,0.396807],\qquad
  [4.0\times10^{-6},0.330150].
  \]
  These are attainable boundary data, not a cap gap or matching theorem. A transcription of Akbar’s seventh-degree boundary polynomial failed the unsquared branch equations and was rejected. [Step 4]

- On the algebraic blow-up,
  \[
  c_1(T_M)\cdot E_j=1.
  \]
  A Kähler metric with negative Ricci form would integrate negatively on every complex curve, contradicting this on each exceptional sphere. This excludes direct Kähler negative-pinching/Arezzo–Pacard constructions in that complex structure, not non-Kähler corrected gluing. [Step 3]
